# Voice Guide: ripgrep

The voice of ripgrep's own documentation, inferred by kapi from README.md, GUIDE.md and FAQ.md at 14.1.1, then corrected by hand.

## Tone
- Personality: knowledgeable peer, not a vendor, patient explainer who shows the reasoning, not just the answer, candid about limits and unknowns, pragmatic: gives the workaround even when the cause is unfixed, generous toward other tools and their users
- Formality: technical
- Emotion: calm and matter-of-fact; enthusiasm reserved for genuinely good news ("Yes!"), mild exasperation permitted at real problems ("Owch.")
- Humor: light
- Guidelines: Calm and matter-of-fact. Enthusiasm is reserved for genuinely good news ("Yes!") and mild exasperation is permitted at real problems ("Owch."). Answer the literal question first, in one word or one sentence when possible ("Yes. See the guide's section on configuration files."), then expand. Explain mechanism when it changes what the reader should do. Say plainly what you do not know rather than bluffing. Never promise dates or outcomes you cannot keep; state the policy and the reason instead. Treat other tools as legitimate choices; explain ripgrep's design on its own rationale. Humor is dry, rare, and arises from the situation, never from a joke inserted for effect.

## Style Rules
- Use active voice
- Sentence length: varied
- Point of view: second
- Contractions: always

## Vocabulary
### Preferred Terms
- **ripgrep**: Always lowercase, including at the start of a sentence: "ripgrep is a project whose contributors are volunteers."
- **rg**: The binary name in commands and transcripts; prose says "ripgrep", shell lines say `rg`.
- **flag**: Dominant word for CLI arguments: "the -U/--multiline flag", "two flags related to colors". "options" appears only when referring to `rg --help` output.
- **-P/--pcre2**: Cite short and long forms together as a slash pair on first mention: -f/--file, -z/--search-zip, -U/--multiline.
- **Note that**: Standard caveat opener, also used parenthetically as "(Note: ...)".
- **regex engine**: Used consistently for both the default and PCRE2; "default regex engine" contrasts with "PCRE2".
- **true color**: Two words, lowercase, for RGB support: "true color support already works out of the box".
- **work around**: Verb is two words ("you can work around by simply increasing the limit"); noun is hyphenated ("The work-around above").

### Forbidden Terms
- ~~Ripgrep~~ → use **ripgrep**: Capitalized forms (Ripgrep, RipGrep, RIPGREP) never appear; the name is lowercase in every one of ~60 occurrences.
- ~~blazing fast~~ → use **a timed comparison, e.g. "real 0m1.783s" vs "real 0m2.458s"**: Performance is always demonstrated with `time` output or `--trace` lines, never asserted.
- ~~we guarantee / we promise~~ → use **"generally", "on a best effort basis", "no promises are made"**: The release-policy entry hedges deliberately: "However, no promises are made."
- ~~utilize~~ → use **use**: "use" throughout: "ripgrep uses parallelism", "Use the --colors flag".
- **simply**
- ~~just~~ → use **say what it takes instead**
- ~~easy~~ → use **say what it takes instead**
- **straightforward**
- ~~under the hood~~ → use **name the module**

### Competitor Terms
- ~~ag~~ → use **The Silver Searcher**: Referred to by full name with the article, and accommodated rather than attacked: an entire entry explains how to emulate its output style.
- **grep**: Named plainly and given its own entry ("Can ripgrep replace grep?"); no put-downs.
- **PCRE2**: A supported alternative engine. Tradeoffs are stated factually ("Both regex engines are quite fast") and unknowns are conceded: "Why doesn't PCRE2 do the same? This author isn't familiar with its internals."
- **cygwin**: Lowercase, described as a source of path-mangling behavior with three concrete fixes offered rather than a verdict.

## Examples
### Example 1
- Before: "RipGrep is a blazingly fast, next-generation search tool that leaves The Silver Searcher in the dust."
- After: "By default, ripgrep uses parallelism to execute its search because this makes the search much faster on most modern systems."
- Why: Lowercase product name, no superlatives, no competitor put-down, and the speed claim is tied to a stated mechanism (parallelism) rather than asserted as branding.

### Example 2
- Before: "The next release is currently scheduled for Q3, though this may slip."
- After: "ripgrep is a project whose contributors are volunteers. A release schedule adds undue stress to said volunteers. Therefore, releases are made on a best effort basis and no dates will ever be given."
- Why: States the policy and the reason behind it instead of a date. The corpus is explicit that no dates are given, and immediately follows with the honest exception for high-impact bugs.

### Example 3
- Before: "It should be noted that users may configure the man page location, and the documentation should then be accessible via standard mechanisms."
- After: "Note that the man page's documentation for options is equivalent to the output shown in rg --help. To see more condensed documentation (one line per flag), run rg -h."
- Why: Bare "Note that", concrete commands instead of abstract "standard mechanisms", and second person addressed through an imperative. Every how-to answer in the corpus lands on a runnable `$` line.

### Example 4
- Before: "Unfortunately, we are unable to provide details on PCRE2's internal behavior at this time."
- After: "Why doesn't PCRE2 do the same? This author isn't familiar with its internals, so we can't comment on it here."
- Why: Candid admission of a limit, in contractions, without corporate hedging or apology. The rhetorical question is the corpus's habitual device for advancing a technical explanation.

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

Globs get repetitive. If you keep typing `rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'`, ripgrep already
has a name for that set of files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

A *type* is nothing more than a name bound to one or more globs. `rust` is
`*.rs`; `go` is `*.go`; `c` is `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in` and `*.cats`. ripgrep
ships with more than 200 such names (`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`), and
several have aliases — `py`/`python`, `md`/`markdown`, `ts`/`typescript`,
`bat`/`batch` are interchangeable.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only these

`-t` is repeatable and the results union: `rg -tpy -tjs TODO` searches Python
*and* JavaScript files. Once any `-t` is in play ripgrep switches to whitelist
mode — a file that matches no selected type is skipped.

Two properties are worth internalising, because they explain most surprises.

**Type globs match the file name, not the path.** ripgrep extracts the base
name and tests the globs against that alone. `*.rs` matches `src/deep/lib.rs`
because the name is `lib.rs`. It also means a type glob containing a `/` can
never match, and that types like `make` work by naming files outright
(`[Mm]akefile`, `*.mk`, `*.mak`).

**Types never apply to directories.** The matcher returns "no opinion" for any
directory, so `-t` filters the files ripgrep reports, it doesn't prune the walk.
Use `-g '!vendor/'` if you want to skip a tree.

`-t` also sits low in the precedence chain. ripgrep consults `-g/--glob`
overrides first and returns immediately on a hit; then ignore-file rules, where
an ignore match also returns immediately; only then types. So a file excluded by
`.gitignore` stays excluded no matter what `-t` you pass — reach for
`-u`/`--no-ignore` to override that, not for a type.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: search everything but these

`-T` is the mirror image: `rg clap -Trust` searches everything except Rust
files, and `-T` is likewise repeatable. Mixing the two is fine
(`rg -ttoml -Tjson pattern`). When a file matches both a selected and a negated
type, **the flag given later on the command line wins** — ripgrep keeps
selections in argument order and the last matching glob takes precedence.

## The special value `all`

`--type all` behaves as if you had passed `-t` for every type ripgrep currently
knows, custom ones included. That is whitelist mode: search only files ripgrep
recognises. `--type-not all` is the inverse — search only the *unrecognised*
files.

The asymmetry catches people. Given `my-shell-script` (no extension) and
`my-shell-library.bash`, both `-tsh` and `-tall` find only the `.bash` file,
since no `sh` glob matches an extensionless name; `-Tall` finds only
`my-shell-script`. `-Tall` is a decent way to spot files ripgrep has no type
for.

## `--type-add`: define your own

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

The format is `name:glob`, one glob per flag, and the flag is repeatable — the
three-flag form (`'web:*.html' 'web:*.css' 'web:*.js'`) is equivalent. Globs
*add* to whatever that name already has, so `--type-add 'py:*.pyx'` extends the
built-in `py` rather than replacing it. To replace, clear first:
`--type-clear py --type-add 'py:*.pyx'`.

There is also an include directive that composes existing types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc pattern
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc pattern
```

Two ordering rules follow from how ripgrep applies these left to right: every
name in an `include:` list must already be defined at that point, and any
`--type-add` you want `-tall` to pick up must come before it.

Names must be Unicode letters or numbers only — no punctuation, and `all` is
reserved. A malformed spec fails with `invalid definition (format is type:glob,
e.g., html:*.html)`; selecting a name that doesn't exist fails with
`unrecognized file type: <name>`, which is also what
`--type-clear rust -trust` gets you.

**Nothing is persisted.** `--type-add` applies to that one invocation. To make a
type permanent, alias it:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or put it in a config file pointed at by `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one shell
argument per line, no escaping:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^go:'
go: *.go
```

Each line is `name: glob, glob, ...`, sorted by name with globs sorted within
each line. It reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` on the same command,
so it doubles as a way to check a definition before you rely on it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list | rg '^web:'
```

It exits nonzero only if there are no definitions left to print. Since types are
searchable text, `rg --type-list | rg yaml` is the fastest way to answer "does
ripgrep know about this format, and under what name?"

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

A file type in ripgrep is just a name attached to one or more file name
patterns. `rust` means `*.rs`. `make` means `*.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile,
Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile`. That's the whole idea. The four
flags below let you use those names, list them, and define your own.

## See what you already have

Start here:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each line is a type name, a `:`, and then a comma-delimited list of the
patterns that make it up. ripgrep ships with more than 200 type names, so pipe
the output through ripgrep itself when you're looking for one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Some types have aliases. `py` and `python` are the same type, as are `md` and
`markdown`. `--type-list` also reflects any types you added or cleared in the
same command, which makes it the fastest way to check a definition you just
wrote.

## `-t/--type`: only these files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

Both forms work; the short flag takes its value with no space. Pass the flag
more than once to search several types at once:

```
$ rg 'TODO' -trust -tmd
```

Naming a type that doesn't exist is an error, not a silent no-op:

```
$ rg -tnope title
rg: unrecognized file type: nope
```

## `-T/--type-not`: everything but these files

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

`-t` means "include files of this type", `-T` means "exclude files of this
type". You can mix them, and here order matters. When a file matches both an
included and an excluded type, the flag written later on the command line
wins:

```
$ rg --type-add 'foo:*.{rs,foo}' -tfoo -Trust title
main.foo:title

$ rg --type-add 'foo:*.{rs,foo}' -Trust -tfoo title
main.foo:title
main.rs:title
```

Note that type filters have lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and
than any rules in your ignore files. If your `.gitignore` excludes a file,
`-t` won't bring it back.

## `--type-add`: define your own

The format is `name:glob`, and one glob per flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

A brace alternation gets you the same thing in one flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

By default, globs are added to whatever ripgrep already defines for that name,
so `--type-add 'md:*.markdown'` extends the built-in `md` type rather than
replacing it. Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers —
`my-web` is rejected — and `all` is reserved.

You can also build a type out of other types with the include directive:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc title
```

Every name after `include:` must already be defined at the point the flag is
read, so put your `--type-add` definitions before any include that uses them.
If one name in the list is bad, the whole definition is rejected and nothing
changes. You can keep adding plain globs to an included type afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' title
```

## What the globs match

Type globs are matched against the file name only, never the full path. So
`--type-add 'web:src/*.js'` will never match anything — use `-g` for path
patterns and save types for names. Types also don't apply to directories.

This is also why a file with no extension slips through most types. A shell
script named `my-shell-script` isn't matched by `-tsh`, because the `sh` globs
all require an extension.

## `--type-clear` and the `all` type

`--type-clear NAME` throws away the existing globs for a type, and you can add
new ones afterward. Order matters:

```
$ rg --type-clear md --type-add 'md:*.markdown' --type-list | rg '^md:'
md: *.markdown
```

Reverse those two flags and the clear wipes out your addition too.

Both `-t` and `-T` accept the special value `all`. `-tall` searches every file
matched by any defined type, custom types included — whitelist mode, where
ripgrep only searches files it recognizes. `-Tall` is the inverse: it searches
only the files no type recognizes. That's the fast way to find your
extensionless scripts, stray data dumps, and anything ripgrep doesn't have a
name for yet.

## Making a type stick

`--type-add` and `--type-clear` apply to the current command only. Nothing is
persisted. To get a type in every invocation, either alias it:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or put it in your configuration file, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

ripgrep reads that file from the path in `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, and it won't
look anywhere else. Once it's there, `-tweb` works everywhere, and
`--type-list` will show `web` alongside the built-ins.

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

A *file type* in ripgrep is just a name attached to one or more globs. `rust`
means `*.rs`; `c` means `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in` and `*.cats`. Instead of
retyping `-g '*.{c,h}'` on every search, you name the set once and reuse it.
ripgrep ships with just over 200 built-in type definitions, and a handful have
aliases — `py` and `python`, `md` and `markdown`, `ts` and `typescript`,
`bat` and `batch` — so you can spell them the way you think of them.

## `-t/--type`: search only these files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust          # short form; the value attaches directly
```

Repeat the flag to widen the net — multiple `-t` flags are OR'd:

```
$ rg TODO -trust -tmd
```

The moment you pass a single `-t`, ripgrep switches into whitelist mode: a file
that matches no selected type is skipped. This is the flag's real value on a
large tree — you are not just filtering output, you are not opening the files
at all.

`--type=all` is a special value meaning "every type currently defined,
including ones you added on this command line." It is whitelist mode over
ripgrep's whole type table: recognized files get searched, unrecognized ones
don't. A shell script named `my-shell-script` with no extension isn't matched
by the `sh` globs, so `-tall` skips it.

If you name a type that doesn't exist, ripgrep errors out rather than quietly
matching nothing — a typo'd `-tpyton` fails loudly.

## `-T/--type-not`: skip these files

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

`-T` is the mirror image and also repeatable. The asymmetry worth knowing: `-t`
puts everything else out of scope, while a lone `-T` only removes the named
type and leaves everything else searchable as usual.

You can mix them. When a file matches globs from more than one selection, the
**last one on the command line wins**, so ordering is how you carve out
exceptions:

```
$ rg config -tall -Tjson       # every recognized type except JSON
```

`--type-not=all` is the inverse of `--type=all`: it searches only files ripgrep
*doesn't* recognize. That's a good way to find the strays — extensionless
scripts, odd config files — that your type-based searches have been missing.

## `--type-list`: see what a type actually covers

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

One type per line, name, then `: `, then its globs comma-separated; both the
list and each type's globs are sorted. Reach for this before you assume a type
covers what you think — `js` includes `*.vue`, `*.cjs` and `*.mjs`; `css`
includes `*.scss`; `json` includes `composer.lock`. `--type-list` also reflects
any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags in the same invocation, which makes
it the way to check a custom definition before searching with it.

## `--type-add`: define your own

The format is `NAME:GLOB`, one glob per flag, additive to whatever ripgrep
already defines for that name:

```
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' -tweb
$ rg title --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb        # same thing
```

Defining a type does not select it — you still need `-tweb`.

There is also an include directive that composes existing types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc PATTERN
```

Included types must already be defined by the time the flag is parsed, so put
your `--type-add 'wat:*.wat'` before the `--type-add 'combo:include:wat,py'`
that references it. Type names must be only Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation — and `all` is reserved.

The related `--type-clear NAME` wipes a type's globs entirely; you can add new
ones afterward, but `--type-clear rust -trust` with nothing added back is an
error, because `rust` no longer exists.

**None of this persists.** Type settings apply to one invocation only. To keep
a definition, use a shell alias or a config file pointed at by
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Things that will bite you

- **Type globs match the file name only, not the path.** `--type-add
  'foo:src/*.rs'` will never match. Use `-g` for path-shaped patterns.
- **Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** Precedence runs `--glob` first,
  then ignore rules, then types. A gitignored file stays unsearched no matter
  what `-t` you pass; add `-u`/`--no-ignore` if you want it back.
- **Explicit paths bypass filtering.** `rg -tpy foo main.rs` searches
  `main.rs`. Type filtering applies to files ripgrep discovers by walking, not
  to ones you hand it.
- **Types never apply to directories,** so `-t` doesn't prune the traversal —
  it prevents files from being read and searched.

## Quick reference

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-tTYPE` | search only TYPE (repeatable; whitelist mode) |
| `-t all` | search only recognized types |
| `-TTYPE` | skip TYPE (repeatable) |
| `-T all` | search only unrecognized files |
| `--type-add 'N:GLOB'` | add a glob to type N |
| `--type-add 'N:include:A,B'` | build N from existing types |
| `--type-clear N` | drop N's globs |
| `--type-list` | print all types and their globs |

# File-type filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering is the machinery behind `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`,
`--type-add`, `--type-clear` and `--type-list`. It lives almost entirely in the
`ignore` crate, in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. The `core` crate only translates CLI flags
into calls on the builder.

## How type definitions are represented

The shipped types are a single flat constant in `default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]),
    ...
];
```

Each entry is `(aliases, globs)`. Aliases exist only in this table:
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` loops `for name in names { for ext in exts { add(name, ext) } }`,
so `bat` and `batch` become two fully independent definitions that happen to
hold equal glob lists. Nothing at runtime knows they were aliases.

At runtime a type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }` — a
name and a list of glob *strings*, uncompiled. `TypesBuilder` holds
`types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` plus an **ordered**
`selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`, where `Selection` is
`Select(name, T) | Negate(name, T)`. Definitions and selections are deliberately
separate: defining a type does not select it.

`TypesBuilder::add(name, glob)` rejects the name `all` and any name containing a
non-`is_alphanumeric` character (`Error::InvalidDefinition`) — which is why no
default type is named `c++` or `objective-c`. It *appends* to an existing
definition rather than replacing it; only `clear(name)` removes one.

`add_def` parses the user-facing string forms: `name:glob`, and
`name:include:a,b,c`. The `include` form is resolved **eagerly** — it clones the
globs of `a` and `b` into the new type, so it is a snapshot, not a live
reference; later edits to `a` don't propagate. It validates that every named
type exists *before* copying anything, so a failed `add_def` never leaves a
half-built definition (asserted by `test_invalid_defs`).

## How the matcher is built

`TypesBuilder::build()` walks `self.selections` in order. For each selection it
looks up the definition (missing → `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`), compiles each
of its globs with `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` into one
shared `GlobSetBuilder`, and records `glob_to_selection.push((isel, iglob))`.
Only *selected or negated* types contribute globs; unselected definitions are
carried along in `Types::defs` purely so `--type-list` can print them.

The resulting `Types` holds the compiled `GlobSet`, the `selections` (now
`Selection<FileTypeDef>`), the `glob_to_selection` side table, `has_selected`
(true if any selection is non-negated), and `matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` — a
pooled scratch buffer so per-path matching doesn't allocate. `Types` is cheap to
clone and is shared as `Arc<Types>` by the walker.

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` is the whole matching algorithm:

1. Directories and an empty glob set return `Match::None`. **File types never
   apply to directories**, so a type filter cannot prune a subtree.
2. It matches only `file_name(path)` (from `pathutil.rs`), never the full path.
   That is why bare-name globs like `CMakeLists.txt`, `BUILD` and `alire.toml`
   work. If `file_name` returns `None` (paths ending in `.` or `..`), the result
   is `Ignore` when `has_selected`, else `None`.
3. `set.matches_into` fills the scratch vec with matching glob indices in
   ascending order; the code takes `matches.last()`. Since indices are assigned
   in selection order, **the last selection on the command line wins**. So
   `-tfoo -Trust` and `-Trust -tfoo` genuinely differ for a file matching both.
4. A hit maps back through `glob_to_selection` to its `Selection`, yielding
   `Match::Ignore` if negated and `Match::Whitelist` otherwise.
5. No hit: `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` if `has_selected` (this is
   "whitelist mode" — the reason `-tall` restricts to recognized files), else
   `Match::None`. Note `Glob::file_type_def()` returns `None` in this case;
   callers must handle it.

## Wiring into ripgrep

`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs:1177` builds the matcher: `add_defaults()`, then
replays `low.type_changes` — a *single* ordered `Vec<TypeChange>` of
`Clear | Add | Select | Negate`. Because it is one ordered stream,
`--type-clear rust -t rust` is an error, while the reverse order is not (see the
`file_type_clear` integration test).

The matcher flows through `WalkBuilder::types` → `IgnoreBuilder::types` →
`Arc<Types>`. In `crates/ignore/src/dir.rs:399`, types are consulted *after*
`--glob` overrides and *after* ignore-file rules, and only when
`!types.is_empty()`. Careful: `Types::is_empty()` means "zero selections", not
"zero definitions". An ignore-file `Ignore` short-circuits before types are
consulted, matching the documented precedence in `--type`'s long help.
`--type-list` is handled separately in `main.rs:329`, printing `definitions()`
and exiting 1 if there are none.

## What a contributor needs to know

- **Adding a default type**: append to `DEFAULT_TYPES`, keep it sorted by first
  alias (`default_types_are_sorted` enforces this) and wrapped to 79 columns.
- Globs accumulate, and overlap is expected and fine — both `c` and `cpp` claim
  `*.h`, and both `config` and `bitbake` claim `*.conf`.
- `select("all")` / `negate("all")` iterate `HashMap` keys, so the *order* of the
  expanded selections is nondeterministic. The verdict is stable (all entries are
  the same kind), but which `FileTypeDef` gets reported for a multi-type file is
  not — don't build behavior on it.
- Test coverage: the `matched!` macro in `types.rs`'s test module for unit
  behavior; `tests/misc.rs` (`file_types*`, `file_type_add*`, `type_list`) for
  end-to-end behavior.

# File type filtering

File type filtering lives in the `ignore` crate, in two modules: `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` (the machinery) and `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs` (the data). Nothing else in the workspace implements type matching; `crates/core` only translates flags into builder calls.

## How definitions are represented

A definition is a name plus a list of globs:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef {
    name: String,
    globs: Vec<String>,
}
```

That's the whole model. There's no extension list, no content sniffing, no MIME table — a "type" is a name bound to globs, and membership is decided by matching a path's file name against them.

The defaults are a flat const table in `default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["ada"], &["*.adb", "*.ads"]),
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    ...
];
```

The first slice is names, the second is globs. Multiple names in the first slice are aliases, but only in the sense that `add_defaults` loops over the cross product and calls `add(name, glob)` once per pair. There's no alias indirection at runtime: `bat` and `batch` become two independent `FileTypeDef` values with identical globs, and both show up separately in `--type-list`. Note that globs are file-name globs, not path globs — `matched` extracts the file name before matching, so a definition like `*.rs` and a definition like `src/*.rs` behave differently only in that the latter can never match.

`TypesBuilder` holds definitions in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` keyed by name, and selections in a separate `Vec<Selection<()>>`. Definitions and selections are independent: defining a type does not select it, and `build()` only compiles globs for types that were actually selected or negated.

## How the matcher is built

`TypesBuilder::build()` walks `self.selections` in order. For each selection it looks up the named definition — a miss is `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` — and then adds every glob of that definition to a `GlobSetBuilder` with `literal_separator(true)`. As it goes it pushes `(isel, iglob)` onto `glob_to_selection`, so glob index *i* in the compiled `GlobSet` maps back to the selection that contributed it.

That parallel-index trick is the load-bearing part of the design. `Types::matched` calls `GlobSet::matches_into`, which returns matching glob indices **in ascending order**, and then takes `matches.last()`. Because `glob_to_selection` was built in selection order, the highest glob index is the *last* selection on the command line that matched. Precedence is therefore last-flag-wins, and it falls out of the index ordering rather than from any explicit comparison. If you reorder how globs are added to the set, you break precedence silently.

The rest of `matched` is small and worth reading in full:

- Directories never match; `is_dir` returns `Match::None` immediately, as does an empty glob set.
- `has_selected` is precomputed at build time as "at least one non-negated selection exists." When it's true, a non-match becomes `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` rather than `Match::None` — this is what makes `-t rust` a whitelist instead of a mere preference.
- `pathutil::file_name` returns `None` for paths that are empty or end in `.` or `..`; that case follows the same `has_selected` rule.
- A matching selection yields `Match::Whitelist` or `Match::Ignore` depending on `Selection::is_negated`.

`Types` also carries `matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` from `regex_automata`'s pool, so the per-match scratch vector isn't reallocated on every path during a parallel walk. Keep that in mind if you add state to `Types`: it's cloned per worker in `dir.rs`.

## Where it plugs in

`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()` builds the matcher. It calls `add_defaults()` and then replays `low.type_changes` — a single `Vec<TypeChange>` covering `--type-clear`, `--type-add`, `-t/--type` and `-T/--type-not` — in argument order, which is why `--type-clear cpp --type-add 'cpp:*.foo'` works but the reverse doesn't.

The result reaches the walker via `WalkBuilder::types` → `IgnoreBuilder::types`, stored as `Arc<Types>`. In `Ignore::matched` (`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs:399`), types are consulted **last**: `-g/--glob` overrides win outright, then ignore-file rules, then types. That ordering is what the `-t` documentation means by "lower precedence than both the --glob flag and any rules found in ignore files."

## What to know before changing this

- **`add` validates names, not globs.** A name must be non-empty, not `all`, and every character must satisfy `char::is_alphanumeric`; otherwise you get `Error::InvalidDefinition`. Glob syntax errors surface later, at `build()`, as `Error::Glob`.
- **`include` is a snapshot, not a reference.** `add_def("bar:include:foo,cpp")` clones the globs of `foo` and `cpp` into `bar` right then. Adding globs to `foo` afterwards does not update `bar`. `add_def` also validates all included names up front so a partial failure can't mutate state — `test_invalid_defs` asserts exactly that.
- **`select("all")` / `negate("all")` iterate `HashMap` keys**, so the relative order of the pushed selections is unspecified. Don't write code (or tests) that depends on which `FileTypeDef` gets reported when several match under `--type=all`.
- **`clear(name)` removes the definition outright.** A later `select` on that name fails at `build()` rather than matching nothing.
- **Adding a default type** means editing `DEFAULT_TYPES` only. Keep it sorted by first name — `default_types_are_sorted` enforces it — and wrapped to 79 columns. Overlapping globs across types are fine and common (`*.cs` appears under both `cs` and `csharp`).

# File-type filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering is what makes `rg -trust foo` search only Rust files. It lives
entirely in the `ignore` crate, in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`, and is wired into the CLI from
`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs`.

## How definitions are represented

The shipped types are a flat table in `default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]),
    ...
];
```

Each row is `(names, globs)`. The first element is a *list* of names, so a single
glob set can be registered under several aliases (`cs`/`csharp`, `py`/`python`).
`TypesBuilder::add_defaults` iterates the table and calls `add(name, glob)` for
every name × glob pair — aliases are duplicated definitions, not shared
references, so there are currently 202 rows but more names than that.

At runtime a definition is just a name plus its globs:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }
```

`TypesBuilder` holds a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` of definitions and a
separate, *ordered* `Vec<Selection<()>>` of what the user asked for
(`Selection::Select(name)` or `Selection::Negate(name)`). Keeping selections in a
vec rather than a set is what gives last-flag-wins precedence, described below.

`add` rejects the reserved name `all` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric
character (`Error::InvalidDefinition`). `add_def` parses the two user-facing
string forms: `name:glob` and `name:include:a,b,c`. The `include` form is
expanded eagerly at parse time — it copies the globs out of the referenced
definitions — so it can only reference types already defined, and later changes
to `cpp` will not propagate into a `src:include:cpp` defined earlier. `add_def`
validates that *all* referenced names exist before adding anything, so a partly
valid include leaves the builder untouched (asserted by `test_invalid_defs`).

Note that `select("all")` and `negate("all")` also expand eagerly, over whatever
is defined at that moment. `--type-add` after `-tall` is therefore not selected.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build` walks the selections in order and, for each one, resolves
the name against the definition map (missing name → `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`,
which is how `--type-clear rust -trust` fails). Every glob of every selected
definition is pushed into one shared `GlobSetBuilder`, compiled with
`literal_separator(true)`, and a parallel `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`
records which selection (and which glob within it) each set index came from. The
result is a single `GlobSet` covering selects and negations alike — the
select/negate distinction is recovered after matching, not encoded in the set.

`Types` also caches `has_selected` (true if any selection is a select) and an
`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` of scratch buffers for match results, so matching
allocates nothing per call and is safe to share across the parallel walker's
threads. `Types` is `Clone`; `hiargs.rs` clones it into the `WalkBuilder`, and
`dir.rs` wraps it in an `Arc`.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)`:

1. Returns `Match::None` immediately for directories or an empty glob set. Types
   never prune directories — a `-trust` walk still descends everywhere.
2. Extracts the **base name** via `pathutil::file_name` and matches only that.
   Type globs are basename globs; a glob containing `/` will never match.
3. Calls `set.matches_into(name, &mut matches)`, which yields matching indices in
   ascending order. The **last** index wins, since set indices follow selection
   order — so the last `-t`/`-T` flag on the command line decides.
4. If the winning selection is a negation → `Match::Ignore`, else
   `Match::Whitelist`, each carrying a `Glob` that exposes the responsible
   `FileTypeDef`.
5. If nothing matched: `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` when `has_selected`
   (whitelist mode — anything unrecognized is excluded), otherwise `Match::None`.
   The same fallback applies when `file_name` returns `None` (paths ending in `.`
   or `..`).

`Ignore::matched` in `dir.rs` consults types *after* `--glob` overrides and after
ignore-file rules, and only when `!types.is_empty()` (i.e. there is at least one
selection). That ordering is the source of the documented precedence: `-g` and
`.gitignore` both outrank `-t`.

## What a contributor should know

- **Adding a default type**: append a row to `DEFAULT_TYPES`, keep the list
  sorted lexicographically by the *first* alias (enforced by the
  `default_types_are_sorted` unit test) and wrapped to 79 columns. Glob syntax is
  globset's, including character classes such as `*.[chH]`.
- **Matching is case-sensitive**: `case_insensitive` is never set here, which is
  why `asm` lists both `*.s` and `*.S`.
- **Order is semantics.** Anything that reorders `TypesBuilder::selections`, or
  the order globs enter the `GlobSetBuilder`, silently changes precedence.
  `glob_to_selection` must stay index-aligned with the set.
- **`Error::InvalidDefinition` carries no detail**; if you extend `add_def`
  parsing, expect to improve the error type too.
- Tests live in `types.rs` (`matched!` macro over a synthetic type table) and end
  to end in `tests/misc.rs` (`file_type_add`, `file_type_add_compose`,
  `file_type_clear`, `type_list`). `--type-list` prints `Types::definitions()`,
  which is sorted by name with globs sorted within each definition, from
  `crates/core/main.rs`.

keep noise out of your results. ripgrep's file-type flags do the same job
without retyping extension lists: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and
`--type-list` let you say "only Rust files" using a short, memorable name.

## The four flags at a glance

- `-t`/`--type TYPE` — only search files matching `TYPE`.
- `-T`/`--type-not TYPE` — do not search files matching `TYPE`.
- `--type-add TYPESPEC` — define (or extend) a type for the current command.
- `--type-list` — print every type ripgrep knows about, along with the globs
  behind it.

Under the hood, a "type" is just a name bound to one or more glob patterns.
`--type rust` is shorthand for `-g '*.rs'`, and saves writing out the glob for
types that cover several extensions, like C, which needs both `*.c` and
`*.h`.

## `--type`: search only matching files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust        # short flag, value glued on
```

Multiple `--type` flags can be given, and they combine additively — each adds
more files to the search rather than narrowing it further. This is also how
`-t` differs from a glob you write yourself: it's a name for "one or more
globs that match the relevant files," so a single type can stand in for a
whole family of extensions. For instance, ripgrep's built-in `c` type covers
`*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in`, and `*.cats` in one name, and `make` covers eight
filename patterns (`Makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `*.mk`, `*.mak`, and case
variants) so you don't have to enumerate them with `-g`.

`--type` also accepts the special value `all`, behaving as though `--type`
were passed for every file type ripgrep knows, including any added with
`--type-add`. This puts ripgrep in a "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
it recognizes via its type definitions, skipping extensionless or otherwise
unrecognized files. A shell script named `my-shell-script` (no extension)
isn't matched by the `sh` type's globs, so neither `--type sh` nor
`--type all` would search it — only a file like `my-shell-library.bash`
would.

One subtlety: `--type` has lower precedence than both `--glob` and any rules
in your ignore files, so a `.gitignore` exclusion or an explicit `-g` wins
over `--type`.

## `--type-not`: exclude matching files

`--type-not` (short form `-T`) is the mirror image of `--type` — everything
that would normally be searched is searched *except* files of the given
type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

As the project's own guide puts it: `-t` means "include files of this type,"
`-T` means "exclude files of this type." You can mix both in one command —
`-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` negates `rust` and `json` while selecting `toml`.

`--type-not` also understands `all`, flipping `--type all`'s whitelist into a
"blacklist" for *unrecognized* files: `--type-not all` would search
`my-shell-script` (no recognized extension) but skip
`my-shell-library.bash` (recognized by the `sh` type).

## `--type-add`: define your own types

ripgrep ships with a large set of built-in types (on the order of 200 names,
covering everything from `agda` to `zig`), but you'll want one it doesn't
have, or a grouping that spans several existing types. `--type-add` takes a
`TYPESPEC` of the form `name:glob` and adds that glob to the named type,
creating the type if it doesn't already exist. Only one glob can be added per
flag, but you can repeat the flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

This creates a new `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files (brace
expansion lets one flag do what would otherwise take three), then searches it
for `title`. Type names may only contain Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation.

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive that pulls in the globs
from other, already-defined types, useful for building composite types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' PATTERN
```

More globs can still be added to `src` with another `--type-add`. Pair this
with `--type-clear TYPE` to strip a built-in type's existing globs before
adding your own instead of extending them.

The important caveat: `--type-add` is not persistent — it only affects the
current invocation. To make a custom type available everywhere, alias it in
your shell (`alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"`) or add
`--type-add` and its value as two lines in a ripgrep configuration file
(pointed to by the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable).

## `--type-list`: see what's available

`--type-list` prints every type ripgrep currently knows — built-in types plus
anything you've added with `--type-add` (and minus anything removed with
`--type-clear`) — one per line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

This is the fastest way to check whether a type you're about to pass to
`-t`/`-T` exists and exactly which files it pulls in — useful before
`--type-add`ing a duplicate, before relying on `--type all`/`--type-not all`,
or to confirm a custom type registered correctly.

## Putting it together

A typical workflow: check `rg --type-list` for the name you need, use `-t`/`-T`
day to day instead of hand-written globs, and reach for `--type-add` — backed
by a shell alias or config file entry — for recurring, project-specific
groupings not worth retyping as a glob every time.

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`)
to narrow a search to one kind of file. ripgrep's file-type flags do the
same job, but with a name instead of a pattern to remember and retype.
This guide covers the four flags that make up that system: `--type`/`-t`,
`--type-not`/`-T`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## The basic idea: `--type`/`-t`

`--type` limits ripgrep to files matching a named type. A type is just a
name bound to one or more globs. Instead of writing:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

you write:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

or the longer form:

```
$ rg 'int main' --type c
```

`-t` and its type name can be run together (`-trust`) or passed as separate
arguments (`-t rust`, `--type rust`). You can pass `--type` more than once;
each one adds another type to search, so `rg foo -tc -tcpp` searches both C
and C++ files.

Note that `--type` has *lower precedence* than both `-g`/`--glob` and any
rules found in your ignore files. A `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
`-g '!*.rs'` can still exclude a file even if it matches a type you've
selected.

## Excluding a type: `--type-not`/`-T`

`--type-not` is the mirror image: `-t` means "include files of this
type," `-T` means "exclude files of this type."

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

Like `--type`, `--type-not` can be repeated, and `-t`/`-T` flags can be
mixed in one invocation — `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` excludes Rust and JSON
while including TOML.

## Listing what's available: `--type-list`

Before filtering by a type, it helps to know what it actually matches.
`--type-list` prints every supported type, one per line, as a name
followed by a colon and a comma-separated list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known
public formats — things like `rust`, `py`/`python`, `markdown`/`md`, `c`,
`cpp`, and `go` (run `--type-list` with no other arguments for the full,
current set). `--type-list` also takes into account any `--type-add` or
`--type-clear` flags on the same command line, so it reflects the types
actually in effect for that invocation, not just the built-in defaults.

## Defining your own types: `--type-add`

If none of the built-in types fit, `--type-add` lets you define one. It
takes a single `name:glob` pair, and only one glob per flag — pass
`--type-add` multiple times (or use brace expansion) to add several globs
to the same name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

This defines a `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files, then searches
it for `title`. Unless you've used `--type-clear` (below), globs added
with `--type-add`
go *on top of* any existing globs for that name — including built-in
types. So `--type-add 'rust:*.rspec'` extends, rather than replaces, the
existing `rust` type.

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive, letting a new type
pull in the rules of other already-defined types by name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

This defines `src` as everything matched by the `cpp`, `py`, and `md`
types, plus `*.foo` — additional `--type-add` flags keep extending it.
Type names may only contain Unicode letters and numbers, no punctuation.

**`--type-add` is not persistent.** It only affects the invocation it's
passed to; ripgrep does not remember custom types between runs. To make a
custom type available every time, either alias the flag into your shell
(`alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"`) or add
`--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` as a line in your ripgrep configuration
file (set via the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable), which
ripgrep prepends to every invocation's arguments.

A related flag, `--type-clear TYPE`, removes the globs previously defined
for a type name — including built-in ones — without removing the name
itself, so you can redefine it from scratch. Like `--type-add`, it must be
passed on every invocation.

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`, which
behaves as if you'd passed the flag once for every type ripgrep knows
about, including any you defined with `--type-add`.

- `--type all` (equivalent to `-t agda -t asciidoc -t asm ...` for every
  known type) puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
  it recognizes via *some* type definition.
- `--type-not all` puts it into "blacklist" mode: it searches only files
  that *don't* match any known type.

This distinction matters for files without a telltale extension. Given an
extension-less shell script `my-shell-script` that sources a library
`my-shell-library.bash`, both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search
only `my-shell-library.bash` — the `sh` type's globs require an extension.
`rg --type-not all` does the reverse: it searches `my-shell-script`
(unrecognized by any type) but skips `my-shell-library.bash`.

## Putting it together

A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to check a type's globs or
confirm a name exists, reach for `-t`/`-T` in day-to-day searches, and fall
back to `--type-add` (aliased or in your config file) for a recurring
search over files that don't map onto a built-in type. For one-off or
highly specific filename patterns, `-g`/`--glob` still wins on precedence
and needs no type definition — the two mechanisms complement each other.

# Filtering ripgrep Searches by File Type

If you search text for a living, you already know the pain of a glob that
almost matches: `*.c` misses your header files, `*.js` misses your JSX, and
typing the same pattern into every command gets old fast. ripgrep solves this
with a built-in notion of file *types* — named groups of glob patterns you can
select or exclude with a single flag. This guide covers the four flags that
make up that system: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only matching files

`--type` (short form `-t`) limits ripgrep to files matching a given type name.
Instead of writing out a glob every time you want Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

you use the type name directly:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The value of `--type` is just a name assigned to one or more globs, which
lets one name stand in for a whole family of extensions. Searching C files
normally means matching both source and header files:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

but the `c` type already covers that:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

*any* of the named types. Note that `--type` has lower precedence than both
`--glob`/`-g` and any rules found in ignore files — an explicit `--glob`
exclusion or a `.gitignore` rule can still remove a file that a `--type`
selection would otherwise include.

`--type` also accepts the special value `all`, which behaves as though every
supported type — including any you defined yourself with `--type-add` — had
been passed with `--type`. This puts ripgrep into a strict "whitelist" mode:
only files recognized by *some* type definition are searched. That matters
for extensionless files. A shell script named `my-shell-script` with no
extension won't match the globs behind the `sh` type (which look for
extensions like `.sh` or `.bash`), so neither `--type sh` nor `--type all`
will search it, even though both would search a sibling file named
`my-shell-library.bash`.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: exclude matching files

`--type-not` (short form `-T`) is the mirror image: it excludes files
matching the given type rather than requiring them. Grepping for `clap`
across everything except Rust source:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type," and the two can be combined and repeated in a single command
(e.g. `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson`) to build up an inclusion/exclusion set. Like
`--type`, `--type-not` also accepts `all`, but with the opposite effect:
`--type-not all` searches only files that are *unrecognized* by any type
definition — a "blacklist" mode. Continuing the shell script example,
`--type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` (no extension, no matching
type) but skip `my-shell-library.bash` (which does match the `sh` type).

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

Type names are only useful if you know what globs back them, and that's
what `--type-list` shows. Each line is a type name, a colon, and a
comma-delimited list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

`--type-list` reflects the *current invocation's* type definitions, meaning
it takes any `--type-add` or `--type-clear` flags on the same command line
into account — handy for confirming a custom type before you rely on it in a
real search.

## `--type-add`: define your own types

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types for well-known formats,
but you aren't limited to them. `--type-add` adds a glob to a type name,
creating the type if it doesn't already exist. Only one glob per flag, but
you can repeat the flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

or use brace expansion to do it in one flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive that pulls in the rules
of other existing types by name, so you can compose a type out of others and
still add more globs afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers — no punctuation.

The important caveat: `--type-add` (and `--type-clear`, which removes a
type's existing globs before you add new ones) only affects the current
command. Nothing is persisted. If you want a custom type available every
time, define a shell alias (`alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"`)
or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.

## Putting it together

For day-to-day searching, `--type-list` is your reference, `--type-add`
extends it for your project's conventions, and `--type`/`--type-not` are
what you actually type on the command line — reach for `all` on either when
you want a strict whitelist or blacklist based on ripgrep's file-type
recognition rather than a single named type.

# File-type filtering in ripgrep

This covers `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` (and its data file
`default_types.rs`), which implements `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`,
`--type-add`, `--type-clear`, and `--type-list`, plus the glue in
`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` and `crates/core/main.rs` that connects CLI
flags to it.

## Representation: `FileTypeDef` and `TypesBuilder`

A file type is a name paired with glob strings:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }
```

`TypesBuilder` holds mutable state while definitions are assembled:

```rust
pub struct TypesBuilder {
    types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<()>>,
}
```

`types` maps a name (`"rust"`) to its `FileTypeDef`. `selections` is the
ordered list of select/negate requests, recorded independently of whether
the name currently exists in `types`.

`add_defaults()` populates `types` from `DEFAULT_TYPES` in
`default_types.rs` — a `const` slice of `(&[&str] names, &[&str] globs)`
pairs, which a comment asks contributors to keep lexicographically sorted
and wrapped to 79 columns. One entry can register several names for the
same globs (e.g. `(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`).

`add(name, glob)` requires `name` to be non-empty, Unicode
letters/numbers only, and not `"all"` (reserved, see below); it appends
`glob` to that name's `FileTypeDef`, creating it via `HashMap::entry` if
needed. `add_def(spec)` parses the `--type-add` string form, split on `:`:

- `name:glob` — a plain association (`"foo:*.foo"`).
- `name:include:other1,other2` — copies every glob currently registered
  under each listed name into `name`. The referenced names are validated
  up front (`types.contains_key`) so a bad reference fails before anything
  is mutated; `test_invalid_defs` asserts a rejected `add_def` leaves
  `definitions()` unchanged.

`select`/`negate` push `Selection::Select`/`Selection::Negate`. Both
special-case `name == "all"` by pushing one selection per key currently in
`types` — so `--type all` snapshots whatever names exist *at the time it
runs*, meaning it must come after the `--type-add`s that should count.
`clear(name)` only removes the entry from `types`; it does not touch
`selections`.

## Building a matcher: `Types`

`TypesBuilder::build()` produces an immutable `Types`:

```rust
pub struct Types {
    defs: Vec<FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>,
    has_selected: bool,
    glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>,
    set: GlobSet,
    matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>,
}
```

It walks `self.selections` **in recorded order**, resolving each name
against `self.types` (`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if missing — this is
where selecting a since-`clear`ed name surfaces). Every glob in the
resolved `FileTypeDef` is compiled with `GlobBuilder::literal_separator(true)`
(so `*` never crosses `/`) and added to one shared `GlobSetBuilder`. Each
compiled glob's position is recorded in `glob_to_selection` as
`(selection_index, glob_index)`, the join table used at match time.
`has_selected` precomputes whether any selection is a `Select` (not just
`Negate`s), which drives whitelist-mode semantics.

### Matching: `Types::matched`

```rust
pub fn matched<'a, P: AsRef<Path>>(&'a self, path: P, is_dir: bool) -> Match<Glob<'a>>
```

- Directories always return `Match::None`, as does an empty `GlobSet` —
  type filtering only applies to files.
- Matching uses the **file name only** (`pathutil::file_name`), never the
  full path. No extractable name yields `Match::Ignore` if any selection
  exists, else `Match::None`.
- `GlobSet::matches_into` fills a pooled `Vec<usize>` with indices of every
  matching glob, in ascending order of when each glob was added to the
  set. `matches.last()` is taken as the winner — so when two selections
  both match, whichever `select`/`negate`/`add_def` call happened **later**
  during builder construction wins, including globs pulled in via
  `include:`.
- The winning glob's selection determines the verdict: negated →
  `Match::Ignore`, otherwise `Match::Whitelist`. The result wraps a `Glob`
  referencing the matched `FileTypeDef` (via `Glob::file_type_def()`).
- If nothing matched: `Match::Ignore` when `has_selected` (some positive
  `--type` was requested and this file isn't one of them), otherwise
  `Match::None` (only negations, or no filtering, requested).

`matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` exists only to avoid allocating a
`Vec<usize>` on every call — `Types` is cloned per walker thread and
`matched` runs once per candidate file.

## Where this plugs into the walker

`Types` is never consulted alone. `Ignore::matched` in
`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs` composes it with `-g/--glob` overrides and
gitignore-style rules, highest precedence first:

1. `overrides` (`-g`/`--iglob`) — any non-`None` result returns immediately.
2. gitignore-style rules — an `Ignore` result returns immediately; a
   `Whitelist` is remembered but doesn't short-circuit.
3. `types` — same short-circuit-on-`Ignore`, remember-on-`Whitelist` logic.

The final verdict is whichever whitelist survived if nothing later
overrode it with `Ignore`. This matches the `-t/--type` flag's documented
behavior in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs`: "this flag has lower precedence
than both the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files."

## CLI wiring

`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs` defines `TypeChange` (`Clear`, `Add`,
`Select`, `Negate`); the `Type`, `TypeAdd`, `TypeClear`, `TypeNot` flag
structs in `defs.rs` each push the matching variant onto
`LowArgs::type_changes`, preserving CLI order. `hiargs.rs::types()` replays
that list against a fresh `TypesBuilder` — `add_defaults()` first, then
each `TypeChange` in order — before calling `build()`. `--type-list`
(`Mode::Types` in `main.rs`) calls `args.types().definitions()` and prints
`name: glob, glob, ...`; both `Types::definitions()` and
`TypesBuilder::definitions()` sort output by name (and sort each
definition's globs) purely for display — this sorting is unrelated to, and
doesn't affect, the insertion-order precedence `matched()` uses.

## What a contributor needs to know

- **Adding a default type**: edit `DEFAULT_TYPES`, keep it sorted and
  wrapped, and favor reasonably popular open formats per its doc comment.
- **Precedence is insertion order, not specificity.** Changing where a
  `select`/`negate`/`add_def` call happens in the chain (CLI parsing,
  defaults, includes) changes which glob wins on overlap — decided solely
  by `matches_into` + `.last()`.
- **`clear` doesn't retroactively remove selections.** Clearing a type
  that was already selected/negated defers to a build-time
  `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`, not a silent no-op.
- **`include:` copies globs by value at `add_def` time.** Later `add_def`
  calls extending the source type are not reflected in types that already
  included it.
- **Names are restricted** to Unicode letters/numbers and can't be `"all"`,
  since `"all"` is special-cased by `select`/`negate` to expand to every
  currently-known name.
- Keep the module doctests and the `matched!`-macro unit tests at the
  bottom of `types.rs` in sync with behavioral changes — they're the
  executable spec for whitelist/negate/include interaction.

# File-type filtering internals

This documents `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` (and its companion
`default_types.rs`), the module that backs ripgrep's `-t/--type`,
`--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`, and `--type-list` flags. The
reader is assumed to be comfortable with Rust; this focuses on how the data
is represented and how it flows into a match decision, since that's the part
that isn't obvious from `rg --help`.

## Representation: definitions vs. selections

A file type is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` plus a `globs: Vec<String>`
(`types.rs:146`). Multiple globs can share one name — the built-in `c` type
is `["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]` (`default_types.rs:36`). Definitions
alone don't filter anything; a `Types` matcher only does work once the user
has also *selected* or *negated* one or more names.

`TypesBuilder` (`types.rs:305`) is the mutable, pre-compile side. It holds:

- `types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` — every known definition, keyed by
  name.
- `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>` — the ordered sequence of `select`/`negate`
  calls, storing only the name (`Selection<T>` at `types.rs:185` is generic
  so the builder can defer resolving `T` to a concrete `FileTypeDef` until
  `build()`).

Definitions are populated three ways:

- `add_defaults()` walks the `DEFAULT_TYPES` table in `default_types.rs`, a
  `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` of `(names, globs)` pairs — one glob list can be
  shared by several names, e.g. `(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`
  (`default_types.rs:27`). It's hand-maintained and asked to stay
  lexicographically sorted and wrapped to 79 columns; new formats go here via
  PR.
- `add(name, glob)` (`types.rs:417`) appends one glob to (or creates) the
  named definition. It rejects `name == "all"` and any name containing a
  non-alphanumeric character, since `"all"` is reserved (see below) and type
  names appear unquoted in glob-like CLI syntax.
- `add_def(spec)` (`types.rs:442`) parses the CLI-facing string forms behind
  `--type-add`: `"name:glob"` (2 `:`-separated parts) or
  `"name:include:other,names"` (3 parts, middle literal `"include"`). The
  include form copies every glob from each referenced type into the new one
  at add-time — it does not keep a live link, so a later `--type-add` on
  the source type won't retroactively affect anything that already included
  it. Unknown names in an include list, or a malformed spec, return
  `Error::InvalidDefinition` and leave `self.types` untouched.

## Building the matcher

`build()` (`types.rs:322`) turns the builder into an immutable `Types`. For
each `Selection` in order, it looks up the `FileTypeDef`, and for each of the
def's globs, compiles a `globset::Glob` with `.literal_separator(true)` (so
`*` won't cross `/`) and adds it to a shared `GlobSetBuilder`. It also
records `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`, mapping each compiled
glob's position in the `GlobSet` back to `(selection index, glob-within-def
index)`. A name that isn't in `self.types` produces
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType`; a bad glob produces `Error::Glob`.

The resulting `Types` (`types.rs:165`) stores the compiled `GlobSet`, the
resolved `selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>`, the `glob_to_selection`
index, and `has_selected: bool` — true iff at least one selection is a
`Select` rather than a `Negate`. That flag changes the meaning of "no glob
matched": with only negations active, an unmatched file is fine
(`Match::None`); with at least one positive selection active, ripgrep is in
whitelist mode and an unmatched file is implicitly `Match::Ignore`.

`Types::matched()` (`types.rs:261`) does the actual per-path check. It
extracts the file name only (`pathutil::file_name`) — type matching never
looks at directory components — and calls `GlobSet::matches_into`, which
returns matching glob indices **in ascending order of insertion**. It takes
`matches.last()`, i.e. the *last-added* matching glob, as the highest
precedent, maps it back through `glob_to_selection` to find which
`Selection` won, and returns `Match::Ignore` or `Match::Whitelist`
accordingly, wrapped in a `Glob` that exposes the winning `FileTypeDef` via
`file_type_def()`.

## What a contributor needs to know

**Selection order is precedence order, not just for `select` vs. `negate`.**
Because `matches_into` returns indices ascending and `matched()` takes the
*last* one, if a path matches globs from two different selections, whichever
was pushed into `TypesBuilder.selections` last wins — regardless of whether
it's a select or negate. On the CLI, `type_changes: Vec<TypeChange>` in
`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs` preserves the exact order flags were parsed
in (see `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()`, which replays
`Clear`/`Add`/`Select`/`Negate` in one pass), so flag order on the command
line is meaningful: `rg -t rust -T rust foo` behaves differently from
`rg -T rust -t rust foo`.

**`select("all")` and `negate("all")` iterate a `HashMap`.** Both push one
`Selection` per key in `self.types`, iterating `HashMap::keys()`
(`types.rs:381`, `types.rs:395`), which has no defined order. This is
harmless when every pushed selection agrees (all-select or all-negate,
respectively), but it means the specific `FileTypeDef` reported by
`Glob::file_type_def()` for an "all"-driven match — used e.g. by
`--type-list`-adjacent tooling — isn't deterministic across runs if two
types' globs can match the same file name. Don't rely on which type "wins"
in that case.

**Directories are never matched.** `matched()` returns `Match::None`
immediately when `is_dir` is true (`types.rs:268`), independent of
selections. Type filtering only ever prunes files; directory traversal
pruning is handled elsewhere (overrides and gitignore-style rules in
`ignore::dir`), which is also why `--type` can't be used to skip walking
into a whole directory subtree.

**Precedence relative to other filters is fixed in `dir.rs`, not here.**
`Types` doesn't know about `.gitignore` or `-g/--glob`; `IgnoreInner::matched`
(`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`, ~line 380) checks overrides first (and returns
immediately on any match), then ignore-file rules (returns immediately if
ignored, remembers if whitelisted), then `self.types` last. So type
selections have the *lowest* precedence of the three, matching the
`--type` flag's own documented note ("this flag has lower precedence than
both the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files"). If you change
`Types::matched`'s return semantics, re-check that call site — it treats
`Match::Ignore` from types as final but folds `Match::Whitelist` into a
carried-forward `whitelisted` value that can still be overridden by nothing
(types run last).

**Errors are fail-fast and non-mutating on the builder.** `add_def` checks
all referenced include-names exist *before* calling `add`, and `add` only
ever pushes to `self.types`, never removes — so a rejected `add_def` call
leaves prior definitions untouched (see `test_invalid_defs` in
`types.rs:564`). Preserve that invariant if you touch `add_def`: partial
application of a bad multi-glob spec would silently corrupt subsequent
`--type-list` output.

**`Types::empty()` is the always-off case**, used as the default in
`IgnoreBuilder` (`dir.rs:591`) before `WalkBuilder::types()` is ever called;
its `GlobSet` is empty, so `matched()` short-circuits via `self.set.is_empty()`.

# File-type filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering (`-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`,
`--type-list`) is implemented in the `ignore` crate, not in `ripgrep` itself.
Everything lives in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with the built-in type list
in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. The `core` crate (the `rg` binary)
only parses flags into a small intermediate representation and hands them to
`ignore::types::TypesBuilder`.

## Representation

A single named type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`
(`crates/ignore/src/types.rs:146`). There is no separate AST for glob syntax —
each glob is stored as its original string and only compiled when the matcher
is built.

The built matcher is `Types`:

```rust
pub struct Types {
    defs: Vec<FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>,
    has_selected: bool,
    glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>,
    set: GlobSet,
    matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>,
}
```

`Selection<T>` is `Select(String, T) | Negate(String, T)` — it records both
*which* type a `-t`/`-T` flag referred to and *whether* it was a positive or
negative selection. `set` is a single `globset::GlobSet` containing every glob
from every selected/negated type, built with `literal_separator(true)`.
`glob_to_selection` maps each glob's index in that set back to `(index into
selections, index into that def's globs)`, which is how a match is traced
back to the `FileTypeDef` that caused it. `matches` is a `Pool` of reusable
scratch `Vec<usize>` buffers so `Types::matched` can call
`GlobSet::matches_into` without allocating per path (matching is meant to run
once per directory entry).

## Building a matcher

`TypesBuilder` (`types.rs:305`) accumulates raw definitions in a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` plus an ordered `Vec<Selection<()>>` of
selections/negations (order matters — see below). Key methods:

- `add(name, glob)` / `add_def("name:glob")` — append a glob to a type. Names
  must be all-alphanumeric and not `"all"`, or `Error::InvalidDefinition` /
  the check in `add()` rejects it.
- `add_def("name:include:other1,other2")` — the 3-part form copies the globs
  of already-defined types into a new type. It fails fast (before mutating
  anything) if any referenced type doesn't exist yet, so `add_def` is
  effectively atomic.
- `select(name)` / `negate(name)` — push a `Selection::Select`/`Negate`. The
  special name `"all"` expands *eagerly*, at the moment `select`/`negate` is
  called, into one `Selection` per name currently in `self.types`
  (`select`/`negate` iterate `self.types.keys()`) — it is not resolved lazily
  at `build()` time. Consequently, on the command line, `--type-add
  'foo:*.foo' --type=all` includes `foo` (added before `all` is expanded),
  while `--type=all --type-add 'foo:*.foo'` does not (added after).
- `clear(name)` — removes a type's definition entirely from the map.
- `add_defaults()` — loads `default_types::DEFAULT_TYPES`, a
  `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` of (names, globs) pairs, lexicographically sorted
  and manually curated.

`build()` (`types.rs:322`) does the real compilation: it walks
`self.selections` *in the order they were added*, resolves each to its
`FileTypeDef`, and appends its globs to a `GlobSetBuilder`, recording
`glob_to_selection` entries as it goes. `has_selected` is true iff any
selection is a non-negated `Select`. Because `Types::matched` takes the
*last* matching glob index from `GlobSet::matches_into`, and glob index order
follows selection order, **later `-t`/`-T` flags on the command line take
precedence over earlier ones when their globs overlap the same file name**.

## Matching semantics

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` (`types.rs:261`) returns `Match<Glob<'_>>`:

- Directories are never matched — `is_dir` short-circuits to `Match::None`.
  Type filters can only ever affect regular file selection, never directory
  pruning during the walk.
- Only the file *name* (`pathutil::file_name`) is tested, not the full path
  or any parent directory component.
- If a path has no file name and any type is `Select`-ed, it's `Ignore`d;
  otherwise `None`.
- Otherwise the globs are matched against the name; the highest-precedence
  match (last index) decides `Whitelist` (from a `Select`) or `Ignore` (from
  a `Negate`).
- If nothing matched at all: `Ignore` if `has_selected` (whitelist mode — only
  recognized types pass), else `None` (no opinion).

## Integration into the walker

`ignore::dir::IgnoreBuilder::types()` stores an `Arc<Types>` on the per-
directory `Ignore` state; `WalkBuilder::types()` (`walk.rs:702`) is the public
entry point. Inside `Ignore::matched_dir_entry`/`matched` (`dir.rs:399`),
type-matching is checked *after* `-g/--glob` overrides and ignore-file rules:
overrides return immediately either way; ignore-file `Ignore` results return
immediately, but a `Whitelist` from ignore files is only remembered, not
returned; types are checked last with the same short-circuit-on-ignore,
remember-on-whitelist pattern, and the final verdict is whichever whitelist
survived (or `None`). This is the documented precedence: `--glob` beats
gitignore rules beats `--type`.

## CLI wiring and contributor notes

`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` defines `Type`, `TypeAdd`, `TypeClear`, `TypeNot`,
`TypeList` as `Flag` impls that each push a `TypeChange` (`Select`, `Add`,
`Clear`, `Negate`) onto `LowArgs::type_changes: Vec<TypeChange>` — a flat,
order-preserving log of everything the user typed. `hiargs::types()`
(`hiargs.rs:1177`) replays that log against a fresh `TypesBuilder::new()` (`add_defaults()` first,
then each `TypeChange` in order) and calls `build()`. Because both
`TypesBuilder` and the CLI preserve command-line order end to end, a
contributor adding a new flag or changing evaluation order must keep that
property — reordering `type_changes` before replay, or building selections
out of order, changes which type wins on overlapping globs.

When adding a built-in type, edit `default_types.rs` only: keep entries
lexicographically sorted and wrapped near 79 columns (per the file's own
doc comment), and prefer extending an existing name array (e.g. `["bat",
"batch"]`) over duplicating globs under two separate type names. Tests for
matching/precedence/error behavior live inline in `types.rs`'s `#[cfg(test)]
mod tests`, using the `matched!` macro; add cases there for new selection or
precedence behavior rather than only relying on the CLI-level integration
tests under `tests/`.

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

When you search text for a living, you spend a lot of energy narrowing *where*
to look. ripgrep's file-type filters let you name a set of files once — "Rust
files," "C files," "web files" — and reuse that name instead of retyping globs.
This guide covers the four flags you'll use most: `--type`, `--type-not`,
`--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## What a "type" is

A file type is just a name assigned to one or more globs that match the
relevant files. That's the whole idea. The `rust` type is a name for `*.rs`;
the `c` type covers both C source and headers so you don't have to write
`-g '*.{c,h}'` by hand. ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types,
generally corresponding to well-known public formats.

One detail worth internalizing: type globs are matched against the **file name
only**, not the full path. A type also never applies to directories. So a type
like `sh` (which is defined by extension globs) will not match an
extensionless script named `my-shell-script`.

## `--type` (`-t`): only search this type

`--type TYPE` limits ripgrep to files matching `TYPE`. Search for `fn run` in
Rust files:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust      # short form; -t and the value can be joined
```

You can pass `--type` multiple times to include several types at once
(`-trust -tpython` searches both).

`--type` accepts the special value `all`, which behaves as if you'd passed
`--type` for *every* type ripgrep knows about, including any you added on the
command line. `--type=all` therefore puts ripgrep in "whitelist" mode: it
searches only files it recognizes via its type definitions.

Precedence matters. `--type` has **lower precedence than the `--glob` (`-g`)
flag and than any rules found in ignore files**. Type filtering narrows what
ripgrep already considers searchable; it does not override an explicit glob or
a `.gitignore` rule.

## `--type-not` (`-T`): skip this type

`--type-not TYPE` is the inverse: do not search files matching `TYPE`.

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." You can mix them freely on one command line
(`-Trust -ttoml -Tjson`), and when a file matches conflicting type globs, the
**last matching glob wins**.

`--type-not` also accepts `all`. `--type-not=all` is "blacklist" mode: ripgrep
searches only files that are *unrecognized* by its type definitions. This is
the natural complement to `--type=all` — for example, `--type-not=all` would
search the extensionless `my-shell-script` that `--type=all` skips.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

`--type-list` prints every supported file type and its globs, one type per
line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`. Pipe it through ripgrep itself to inspect a
single type:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Importantly, `--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags
given on the same command line, so it's the way to confirm a custom definition
took effect.

## `--type-add`: define your own types

`--type-add` adds a new glob for a type using the form `TYPE:GLOB`. Only one
glob is added at a time, but you can repeat the flag. Suppose you often search
"web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title      # same thing, condensed
```

Unless you use `--type-clear` first, new globs are *added* to any existing
globs for that type. Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or
numbers — no punctuation.

`--type-add` also supports an `include` directive that imports the rules of
other, already-defined types. To build a `src` type covering C++, Python, and
Markdown, then extend it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc TODO
```

### These settings are not saved

`--type-add` (and `--type-clear`) apply only to the current invocation.
Nothing is persisted. To make a custom type available everywhere, pass it on
every run via a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add a line to your ripgrep configuration file:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Quick reference

- `-t TYPE` / `--type` — search only this type; `all` = whitelist mode.
- `-T TYPE` / `--type-not` — skip this type; `all` = blacklist mode.
- `--type-add 'name:glob'` — define/extend a type (or `name:include:a,b`);
  not persisted.
- `--type-list` — list all types and their globs, honoring your additions.

script named `my-shell-script` (no extension) that sources
`my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search only
`my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` globs don't match an extensionless
name. Conversely, `rg --type-not all` searches `my-shell-script` but not
`my-shell-library.bash`.

of Unicode letters or numbers; punctuation isn't allowed.


plain globs to it afterward:

```

```

```

```

— or put `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` in your configuration file.
