To review the types, run `--type-list`. Each type prints on its own line,
followed by a `:` and a comma-delimited list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

command, so a type you define appears in the output even though it isn't one of
ripgrep's built-ins. That makes `--type-list` the quickest way to confirm a
custom definition matches what you meant before you rely on it.

# Filtering by File Type in ripgrep

When you grep text for a living, you rarely want to search *everything* under a directory — you want the Python, or everything except the JSON. ripgrep ships knowing about file types, so instead of hand-writing globs you can name a type and let it do the matching. This guide covers the four flags that drive that system: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only a type

`-t rust` limits the search to files matching the `rust` type. As the help puts it: "Only search files matching TYPE." A type is just a named set of globs — `rust` means `*.rs`, `py` means `*.py` and `*.pyi`, `js` means `*.js`, `*.jsx`, `*.vue`, `*.cjs`, `*.mjs`, and so on.

You can repeat the flag to widen the net. To search both Rust and Python:

```
rg -t rust -t python foo
```

The short form can be glued to its value, so `-trust` is the same as `-t rust`.

There's a special value, `all`. `--type=all` behaves as if you'd passed `--type` for every type ripgrep knows (including any custom ones you've defined). That puts ripgrep in "whitelist" mode: it searches only files it recognizes via a type definition, and skips anything it can't classify.

One precedence note that matters in practice: `--type` has *lower* precedence than the `--glob` flag and than any rules in ignore files. A `.gitignore` rule or an explicit `-g` still wins over your type selection.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: exclude a type

`-T` is the inverse: "Do not search files matching TYPE." Use it to carve noise out of a search:

```
rg -T json -T lock config
```

Like `-t`, it repeats to exclude several types, and it accepts `all`. `--type-not=all` is "blacklist" mode: ripgrep searches only files it does *not* recognize.

You can freely combine `-t` and `-T` in one command. When a file matches both a selected and an excluded type, **the last matching rule on the command line wins** — order decides the outcome. So `-t rust -T foo`, where a custom `foo` type also covers `*.rs`, excludes `main.rs`, because the negation came later. Keep that in mind when a file could fall under two types.

## `--type-add`: define or extend a type

Type definitions aren't fixed. `--type-add` adds a glob to a type — creating the type if it doesn't exist. There are two forms.

The first is `name:glob`:

```
rg --type-add 'foo:*.foo' -tfoo PATTERN
```

Only one glob per flag — to give a type several globs, repeat `--type-add`. New globs are *added* to whatever the type already had, so extending a built-in type is additive, not a replacement.

The second form pulls in existing types with an `include` directive: `name:include:type1,type2,...`. To make a `src` type covering C++, Python, and Markdown:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
```

The types you reference must already be defined. The built-ins always load first, so referencing `cpp,py,md` works; but if you're referencing your own custom types, define them earlier on the line. You can mix the two forms — add includes, then bolt on extra globs:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

Two constraints worth remembering. Type names must be Unicode letters or numbers only — no punctuation. And **settings don't persist**: `--type-add` applies only to the invocation it's on. To make custom types permanent, put the flags in a ripgrep configuration file (see the `CONFIGURATION FILES` section of the manual) so every run picks them up.

A companion flag, `--type-clear`, wipes the globs for a named type so you can redefine it from scratch. Because rules apply left to right, a `--type-clear foo` must come *before* the `--type-add 'foo:...'` that rebuilds it.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

When you can't remember whether it's `md` or `markdown` (it's both — many types have aliases), ask:

```
rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as `name: glob, glob, ...` — the name, a colon, then a comma-separated list of its globs. ripgrep ships with roughly 200 built-in types. Crucially, `--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` you pass alongside it, so it's the way to confirm a custom definition came out the way you intended:

```
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-list
```

## A few things to know

- Type globs match against the **file name only**, not the full path, and type filtering never applies to directories.
- Selecting or excluding a name ripgrep doesn't know is an error, not a silent no-op — `--type-list` is your check.
- `all` is reserved: you can select or exclude it, but you can't define a type called `all`.

# File-type filtering in `ignore`

ripgrep's `--type`/`--type-not`/`--type-add` machinery lives entirely in the
`ignore` crate, in two files: `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` (the logic) and
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs` (the shipped type list). This note covers
how definitions are represented, how a `Types` matcher is built, and what to
watch for when editing this area.

## Representation

A single type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`
(`types.rs:145`). The name is the label a user passes to `--type` (`rust`,
`cpp`); the globs are the file-name patterns that recognize it. Nothing here is
compiled yet — a `FileTypeDef` is just strings.

The default list is `DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]`
(`default_types.rs`), a static array of `(names, extensions)` pairs, e.g.
`(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`. One entry can bind several *aliases* to the
same glob set; `TypesBuilder::add_defaults` (`types.rs:482`) flattens this by
looping over every `name` × `ext` and calling `add(name, ext)`, so `bat` and
`batch` become two independent `FileTypeDef`s that happen to share globs. The
list is kept sorted lexicographically and 79-column-wrapped by convention;
`#[rustfmt::skip]` means rustfmt will not do this for you.

## Building a matcher

`TypesBuilder` (`types.rs:305`) holds `types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` and
an ordered `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`. Definitions and selections are
distinct: defining a type only makes it *available*; `select`/`negate` decide
what actually filters.

Definitions arrive three ways:

- `add(name, glob)` — appends one glob to the named def, creating it if absent.
  It rejects the reserved name `all` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric
  character (`types.rs:417`), returning `Error::InvalidDefinition`.
- `add_def(def)` — parses the user-facing string form by splitting on `:`
  (`types.rs:442`). Two colons of content mean `{name}:{glob}`; three mean
  `{name}:include:{comma,separated,names}`, which copies the globs of each
  referenced (already-defined) type into the new one. The `include` branch
  checks *all* referenced names exist before copying any glob, so a bad
  reference leaves the builder unchanged (`test_invalid_defs` asserts this
  atomicity).
- `add_defaults()` — bulk-loads `DEFAULT_TYPES`.

`select(name)`/`negate(name)` push `Selection::Select`/`Selection::Negate`
onto the list; the special name `all` expands to a selection per currently
defined type (`types.rs:381`, `:395`). `Selection` (`types.rs:185`) is generic
over its payload so it can carry `()` in the builder and a resolved
`FileTypeDef` in the built matcher.

`build()` (`types.rs:322`) is where strings become a matcher. It walks
`selections` in order; for each, it looks up the definition (missing →
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType`) and compiles every glob with
`GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` into a single `globset::GlobSet`.
`literal_separator(true)` is important: `*` will not cross `/`, so type globs
match against a file name, not a path. Two side tables are produced:
`glob_to_selection`, mapping each glob's index in the set back to
`(selection index, glob index)`, and `has_selected`, true if any selection is a
`Select`. The result `Types` (`types.rs:164`) owns the `GlobSet`, the resolved
selections, those tables, and an `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` scratch buffer for
match results.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` (`types.rs:261`) returns
`Match<Glob>`—`Whitelist`, `Ignore`, or `None`. The rules:

- Directories and an empty glob set short-circuit to `Match::None`; type
  filters never apply to directories.
- Only the file name is matched (`pathutil::file_name`).
- `set.matches_into` collects every matching glob index into the pooled
  buffer. **The last (highest-index) match wins** — precedence is selection
  order, so later `--type`/`--type-not` flags override earlier ones. The
  winning glob's selection decides `Whitelist` (selected) vs `Ignore`
  (negated).
- If nothing matched but at least one type was *selected* (`has_selected`),
  the path is `Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` — selecting a type implicitly
  excludes everything else. With only negations, a non-match is `Match::None`.

`Glob` (`types.rs:110`) reports which `FileTypeDef` produced a match, or
`UnmatchedIgnore` for the implicit-exclusion case. In the wider pipeline
(`dir.rs:399`) a type `Ignore` is final, while a `Whitelist` is held and can
still be overridden by later ignore rules.

## For contributors

- Adding a default type is usually a one-line edit to `DEFAULT_TYPES`; keep it
  sorted and wrapped (rustfmt won't). Aliases are just extra names in the tuple.
- Globs are file-name globs. Because of `literal_separator(true)`, a pattern
  like `src/*.rs` will not behave as a path glob.
- Precedence is *last selection wins*, and `has_selected` flips an unmatched
  path from `None` to `Ignore`; changes to either alter user-visible semantics.
- Definitions are order-independent (a `HashMap`), but `definitions()`
  (`types.rs:367`) clones, sorts globs, then sorts defs by name, so output is
  deterministic — rely on that for tests, not on insertion order.
- Preserve `add_def`'s fail-fast validation; partial application of an
  `include` def is a regression the existing tests guard against.

# File-type filtering in the `ignore` crate

ripgrep's `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, and `--type-add` flags all resolve to
one piece of machinery: the type matcher in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, seeded
from the table in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. This note describes how
that data is shaped, how `TypesBuilder::build` turns it into a `Types` matcher,
and what you need to watch for if you change this area. The reader is assumed to
be comfortable reading Rust.

## How a type definition is represented

A single type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`. That's
the whole model: a name and a list of glob *strings* (not compiled globs). One
type can carry many globs, and several names can point at the same set of globs.

The defaults live in `DEFAULT_TYPES`, typed as
`&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` — a slice of `(names, extensions)` pairs. The `names`
slice holds aliases; for example `(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])` defines two
names sharing one glob. `add_defaults` walks this table and calls
`add(name, ext)` for every name/extension combination, so aliases become
independent `FileTypeDef` entries that happen to hold identical globs.

Note that the "globs" are ordinary globset patterns, not just extensions:
`*.[chH]` (character classes), `*.{c,h}pp` (alternation), and bare filenames
like `CMakeLists.txt`, `BUILD`, or `alire.toml` all appear in the table.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder` holds `types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` and
`selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`. You populate types with `add`, `add_def`,
`clear`, and `add_defaults`, and record what the user asked for with `select`
and `negate`.

`add(name, glob)` validates the name — it must be non-`all` and every character
must satisfy `char::is_alphanumeric`, otherwise you get
`Error::InvalidDefinition` — then appends the glob to that name's entry. Calling
it repeatedly accumulates globs on one type.

`add_def(def)` parses the string forms the CLI exposes. Split on `:`, then:

- two parts (`name:glob`) delegates to `add`;
- three parts (`name:include:a,b,c`) requires `parts[1] == "include"` and copies
  the globs of each named, *already-defined* type into the new one.

The include form is resolved eagerly and by value: it clones the referenced
globs at definition time. So referenced types must exist first (there are no
forward references), and later edits to a source type don't propagate to an
`include` that already copied it. `add_def` also fails fast — it checks that
every referenced type exists before adding anything, so a bad include leaves the
builder unchanged (see `test_invalid_defs`).

`select`/`negate` only push a `Selection::Select`/`Negate(name, ())` — they
store a *name*, not a resolved definition, and they don't check that the name
exists. The special name `all` expands to a selection for every type currently
defined.

Resolution happens in `build`. For each selection it looks the name up in the
`types` map; a miss is `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`. This is the key timing
point: an unknown `-t foo` surfaces at `build`, not at `select`. For each glob
in the resolved def, `build` compiles a `globset::Glob` with
`literal_separator(true)` and adds it to a `GlobSetBuilder`, while pushing
`(selection_index, glob_index)` onto `glob_to_selection`. That vector is the
bridge from "which glob in the combined set matched" back to "which selection
owns it." The `Selection<()>` is mapped to `Selection<FileTypeDef>` so the
matcher carries the definitions it needs.

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob>`. Directories and an empty
glob set short-circuit to `Match::None` — file types don't apply to directories.
Otherwise it extracts the file name (basename only; directory components never
participate) and runs `set.matches_into` to collect every matching glob index
into a per-thread scratch `Vec` borrowed from an `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`, which
keeps the hot path allocation-free and the matcher `Send + Sync`.

Precedence is "last selection wins": glob indices are appended in selection
order, `matches_into` yields them ascending, and `matched` takes `matches.last()`.
A negated selection produces `Match::Ignore`, a positive one
`Match::Whitelist`. If nothing matched but at least one positive selection
exists (`has_selected`), the path becomes `Match::Ignore` — that's what makes
`-t rust` exclude everything that isn't Rust. With no positive selection, a
non-match is `Match::None`. The `dir.rs` walker consults types after ignore
rules, returning early on `Ignore` and otherwise recording a `Whitelist`.

## What a contributor should know

- To add a default, edit `DEFAULT_TYPES`. Keep it sorted lexicographically by
  the first alias — `default_types_are_sorted` enforces this — and wrap to 79
  columns. The block is `#[rustfmt::skip]`, so format it by hand.
- Names are alphanumeric-only, and `all` is reserved.
- Definition errors (bad name, malformed `add_def`) surface at add time;
  unknown *selections* surface at `build`. Keep that split in mind when you
  change error reporting.
- Ordering of selections is semantically meaningful — think about precedence
  before you reorder how the CLI feeds `select`/`negate`.
- Globs use globset syntax with `literal_separator(true)`; matching is against
  the basename only.

# File-Type Filtering in ripgrep

File-type filtering (`--type`/`-t`, `--type-not`/`-T`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`)
lives entirely in the `ignore` crate, in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` with the
built-in list in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. This is the code that
decides, e.g., that `-t rust` restricts a search to `*.rs`. It is worth reading
as two halves: how definitions are represented, and how the runtime matcher is
compiled and queried.

## How definitions are represented

A single type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`. That is
all a type is: a name and a list of glob *strings* (not compiled globs). Types
can share globs freely and a name may map to many globs.

The built-in list is a flat table:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["rust"], &["*.rs"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]),
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    ...
];
```

Note each entry maps a *list of names* to a *list of extensions*: the first
element lets one file type carry aliases (`bat`/`batch`). `add_defaults` simply
iterates the table and calls `add(name, ext)` for every (name, ext) pair, so
aliases become independent `FileTypeDef` entries that happen to share globs.

`TypesBuilder` is the mutable staging area. It holds `types: HashMap<String,
FileTypeDef>` and a `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`. The interesting methods:

- `add(name, glob)` appends one glob to the named def, creating it if absent. It
  rejects `name == "all"` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric character
  (`is_alphanumeric`), returning `Error::InvalidDefinition`. `all` is reserved
  because `select`/`negate` treat it as "every currently defined type."
- `add_def(def)` parses the string form users pass to `--type-add`. Splitting on
  `:` yields either a 2-part `{name}:{glob}` root definition or a 3-part
  `{name}:include:{comma,separated,names}` include. The include form copies the
  globs of already-defined types into the new one; it validates that every
  referenced type exists *before* mutating (`types.clone().any(...)`), so a
  partially valid include leaves state untouched — a property the `test_invalid_defs`
  test pins down.
- `clear(name)` removes a def; `select`/`negate` push a `Selection`.

`Selection<T>` is `Select(String, T)` or `Negate(String, T)`, carrying a name
and (later) the resolved def. In the builder `T = ()`; selections are just names
until build time. Selections are ordered and that order is precedence.

## Building and querying the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build` turns definitions plus selections into an immutable
`Types`. It walks `self.selections` in order; for each, it looks up the def
(unknown name → `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`), and for every glob compiles a
`globset::Glob` with `literal_separator(true)` (so `*` does not cross `/`) into a
shared `GlobSetBuilder`. Crucially it records `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize,
usize)>` — a parallel array mapping each glob's index *in the compiled set* back
to `(selection index, glob index)`. This is the bridge from a raw GlobSet hit to
"which selection, select or negate, owns it." It also precomputes
`has_selected = selections.iter().any(|s| !s.is_negated())`.

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` is the hot path:

1. Directories and empty sets return `Match::None` immediately — types never
   apply to directories.
2. Only the file name is matched (`pathutil::file_name`), not the whole path.
3. `set.matches_into(name, &mut matches)` collects every matching glob index into
   a pooled `Vec<usize>` (a `regex_automata` `Pool`, hence the `Arc<Pool>` and
   `Clone`).
4. **The last match wins** (`matches.last()`) — GlobSet preserves insertion
   order, so this is the highest-precedence selection. Its selection is negated →
   `Match::Ignore`, otherwise `Match::Whitelist`.
5. If nothing matched, the result is `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` when
   `has_selected` (a positive selection exists, so non-matching files are
   excluded) and `Match::None` otherwise (only negations, so unrelated files pass
   through untouched).

The tri-state `Match` matters: `None` means "types have no opinion," letting
other filters decide. In `dir.rs`, `Ig::matched` consults overrides, then
gitignore-style rules, then types, in that precedence order; a type `Ignore`
short-circuits, a type `Whitelist` is remembered but can still be overridden.
The CLI wiring is in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types`, which calls
`add_defaults` then replays `TypeChange` values (Clear/Add/Select/Negate).

## What a contributor should know

- Adding a built-in type is a one-line edit to `DEFAULT_TYPES`; keep it sorted
  lexicographically and wrapped to 79 columns, as the header comment requires.
- Globs match the file *name only* and forbid separator-crossing, so
  path-shaped patterns will not behave as intended.
- Precedence is selection order, resolved as "last matching glob wins," so
  interleaving `-t`/`-T` on the command line is meaningful.
- Any new name must be non-`all` and strictly alphanumeric, and include
  definitions must validate references before mutating. The unit tests at the
  bottom of `types.rs` are the executable spec — extend the `matched!` macro
  cases when you touch matching semantics.

# File Type Filtering in ripgrep: A User Guide

When you search through code, you often want to focus on specific file types. ripgrep makes this easy with its file-type filtering system. This guide explains `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`, and how to use them effectively.

## What Are File Types?

In ripgrep, a *file type* is a named category that groups together related files using glob patterns. For example, the built-in `rust` type matches all `*.rs` files, while the `c` type matches both `*.c` and `*.h` files. Instead of writing glob patterns manually each time, you can use a file type name as shorthand.

ripgrep ships with dozens of built-in file types covering popular programming languages, markup formats, and data interchange formats—everything from JavaScript and Python to YAML and JSON.

## Using `--type` to Include Files

The `--type` flag (short form: `-t`) limits your search to files of a specific type.

### Basic usage

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type rust
rg 'pattern' -trust
```

Both commands search for `pattern` only in Rust files (files matching `*.rs`).

### More complex example

When searching for `int main`, you could write:
```bash
rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

But with file types, it's simpler:
```bash
rg 'int main' -tc
```

The `c` type automatically expands to match both C source files (`*.c`) and header files (`*.h`), and additionally includes `*.C` and `*.H` (uppercase variants).

### Combining multiple types

You can specify `--type` multiple times to search across several file types:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type rust --type python
```

This searches for `TODO` comments in both Rust and Python files.

## Using `--type-not` to Exclude Files

The `--type-not` flag (short form: `-T`) does the opposite—it excludes files of a particular type from your search.

```bash
rg 'console.log' --type-not javascript
rg 'console.log' -Tjs
```

This searches everywhere *except* in JavaScript files. This is useful when you have multiple file types in a directory but want to focus on just a few.

### Combining inclusions and exclusions

You can mix `--type` and `--type-not` in the same command:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-not test
```

This searches for `TODO` in all file types except those named `test` (which typically matches `*.test.ts`, `*.test.js`, etc.).

## Seeing Available Types with `--type-list`

To see all available file types and the glob patterns they match, use `--type-list`:

```bash
rg --type-list
```

This prints the complete list of built-in types, each with its associated glob patterns. For example:

```
agda: *.agda, *.lagda
c: *.[chH], *.[chH].in, *.cats
cmake: *.cmake, CMakeLists.txt
```

You can pipe this to `grep` to search for a specific type:

```bash
rg --type-list | grep '^rust:'
```

This shows the glob patterns that make up the `rust` type.

## Customizing Types with `--type-add`

The `--type-add` flag lets you define custom file types for your current search. This is useful when ripgrep doesn't have a built-in type for what you need, or when you want to group multiple file types together for a single search.

### Basic syntax

```bash
rg --type-add 'mytype:*.ext' 'pattern' -tmytype
```

### Defining a type with multiple globs

If a type needs to match several file extensions, separate them with commas or use glob brace expansion:

```bash
rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' 'title'
```

Or more concisely:

```bash
rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' 'title'
```

Both define a `web` type that matches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. After defining it, you use it like any other type:

```bash
rg --type-add 'config:*.{conf,cfg,ini,toml}' 'database_url' -tconfig
```

### Important: `--type-add` applies only to the current command

When you use `--type-add`, the custom type exists only for that one ripgrep invocation. Once the command finishes, it's gone. If you want a custom type to persist across searches, you have two options:

1. **Create a shell alias:**
   ```bash
   alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
   ```

2. **Add it to your ripgrep configuration file:**
   Create a config file (e.g., `~/.ripgreprc`) and set the environment variable:
   ```bash
   export RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH=$HOME/.ripgreprc
   ```
   
   Then add to your config file:
   ```
   --type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
   ```

## The Special `all` Type

ripgrep provides a special type named `all` that represents every known file type. It's useful in edge cases:

- `rg --type all 'pattern'` searches files that match *any* known file type, including those added with `--type-add`
- `rg --type-not all 'pattern'` searches only files that *don't* match any known type

The second form is particularly useful for finding extensionless scripts or files with custom naming conventions:

```bash
rg --type-not all 'shebang' .
```

This searches for `shebang` in files without recognized extensions, helping you find your shell scripts that lack the `.sh` extension.

## Practical Examples

### Search only documentation and comments

```bash
rg 'FIXME' --type markdown --type plaintext
```

### Find imports, excluding test files

```bash
rg 'import.*package' --type-not test --type-not spec
```

### Search a monorepo's configuration files

```bash
rg --type-add 'configs:*.{yaml,yml,json,toml,ini,conf}' 'redis' -tconfigs
```

### Search Python but exclude vendored dependencies

```bash
rg 'deprecated' --type python --glob '!vendor/**'
```

(Note: `--type` and `--glob` can be combined for precise control.)

## How File Types Work Under the Hood

ripgrep uses file types to efficiently match multiple glob patterns at once. When you specify `--type rust`, ripgrep doesn't run the pattern once for each glob—instead, it uses an internal regex set that matches all globs simultaneously. This keeps searches fast even when a type encompasses many patterns.

File types are defined in ripgrep's source code as sets of glob patterns. The built-in types cover nearly 200 languages and formats, from mainstream languages like JavaScript and Java to specialized formats like Dhall and Fennel. The maintainers add new types as formats gain popularity, but the list is intentionally limited to reasonably well-known formats to keep ripgrep's scope focused.

## Summary

- **`--type`** narrows search to a specific file type
- **`--type-not`** excludes a file type from search
- **`--type-add`** creates a custom type for the current command
- **`--type-list`** displays all available types and their patterns
- Combine types with `-t` (include) and `-T` (exclude) short forms
- Use the special `all` type to match or exclude all known types
- Make custom types persistent via shell aliases or a config file

By mastering file-type filtering, you'll search faster and more accurately, focusing ripgrep's power on exactly the files you care about.

# File Type Filtering in ripgrep

ripgrep includes a file type system that lets you filter searches to specific kinds of files without writing out glob patterns every time. If you find yourself repeatedly searching only Rust files, Python files, or JavaScript files, file type filtering will save you typing and make your commands clearer.

## What are file types?

A file type is a named collection of glob patterns that match related files. ripgrep ships with dozens of predefined types: `rust` matches `*.rs`, `python` matches `*.py`, `c` matches `*.{c,h}`, and so on. Each type corresponds to files you'd likely want to search together. Instead of writing `-g '*.rs'` every time you want to search Rust code, you can write `-trust` (short for `--type rust`).

## Listing available types

To see all available types and the glob patterns they match, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

This prints every built-in type along with the globs that make it up. For example, the `make` type shows:

```
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

This means the `make` type will match any file whose name is `Makefile`, `makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, or ends with `.mak` or `.mk`. If you've added custom types with `--type-add` (covered below), they'll appear in this list too.

## Including files of a specific type

Use `--type` (or `-t` for short) to search only files of a given type:

```
$ rg 'fn main' --type c
```

This searches only C source and header files for `fn main`. The short form saves characters:

```
$ rg 'fn main' -tc
```

You can specify multiple types. `rg pattern -tc -tcpp` will search both C and C++ files. If you specify the same type twice, it's harmless; ripgrep deduplicates selections internally.

A special type called `all` includes every file type listed by `--type-list`, including any custom types you've added on the command line. This is useful when you want to search across all supported file types:

```
$ rg 'import requests' --type all
```

Note that `all` matches based on the type globs themselves. If you have a shell script without a file extension (like a file named `my-script`), it won't match the `sh` type because the `sh` type's globs only match files with shell extensions. But `--type-not all` will match it, because it explicitly excludes files that match the predefined types.

## Excluding files of a specific type

Use `--type-not` (or `-T` for short) to exclude files of a given type from your search:

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not markdown
```

This searches everywhere except Markdown files for `TODO`. The short form:

```
$ rg 'TODO' -Tmd
```

Just like `--type`, you can combine multiple exclusions:

```
$ rg 'import' -Tpy -Tjs
```

This excludes both Python and JavaScript files from the search.

## Defining custom types

If you have file type combinations you use repeatedly, define them on the command line with `--type-add`:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb 'title'
```

This creates a new type called `web` that matches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files, then searches for `title` only in those files. The format is `name:glob`, where `name` is the type name and `glob` is a glob pattern (or multiple patterns separated by commas).

You can define the same type multiple times to add more globs to it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb 'color'
```

This does the same thing as the example above, just split across multiple flags. Custom types you define on the command line appear in `--type-list` output and can be selected or negated just like built-in types.

**Important:** `--type-add` only applies to the current command. It does not save the type permanently. Once the command finishes, the custom type is gone.

## Making custom types permanent

To use custom type definitions in every ripgrep command without retyping them, add them to a ripgrep configuration file. Set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point to your config file, then add your `--type-add` flags to it:

```
$ cat ~/.ripgreprc
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
--type-add=templates:*.jinja,*.jinja2
```

Now `rg -tweb 'class'` will work automatically without having to specify `--type-add` each time. Configuration files let you put each flag and its value on separate lines if you prefer:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
--type-add
templates:*.jinja,*.jinja2
```

You can also create a shell alias:

```
alias rg='rg --type-add "web:*.{html,css,js}"'
```

But a config file is cleaner if you have more than one or two custom types.

## Common examples

**Search Python files only:**

```
$ rg 'def ' --type python
```

**Search everything except vendor directories (which might not be in your `.gitignore`):**

```
$ rg pattern --glob '!vendor/*'
```

**Search test files in multiple languages:**

```
$ rg 'assert' --type rust --type python --type javascript
```

**Search code but not documentation:**

```
$ rg 'TODO' --type-not markdown --type-not rst --type-not tex
```

**Create a "config files" type and use it:**

```
$ rg 'database:' --type-add 'config:*.{yml,yaml,json,toml,conf}' --type config
```

## How type filtering interacts with other filters

Type filtering works alongside ripgrep's other filtering mechanisms. If you specify a file type with `--type`, ripgrep still respects your `.gitignore` rules and still excludes binary files by default. So `rg pattern --type rust` will skip:

1. Files that don't match the `rust` type globs
2. Rust files listed in your `.gitignore`
3. Binary files (unless you pass `-a/--text`)
4. Hidden files (unless you pass `--hidden`)

You can combine type filtering with glob filtering. `rg pattern --type rust -g '!test_*.rs'` searches Rust files but excludes any whose name starts with `test_`. Later globs override earlier ones, just as they do when using `-g` alone.

## Performance considerations

Type filtering has minimal performance overhead. ripgrep uses the glob patterns that make up each type to quickly determine which files to search, then applies the same parallelism and optimizations it uses for any other search. Using `--type rust` is essentially equivalent to using `-g '*.rs'`, but shorter to type.

## When to use types vs. globs

Use file types when:

* You're searching a well-known file type (Rust, Python, JavaScript, etc.)
* You want to search multiple related extensions as a unit (C type matches both `.c` and `.h`)
* You define custom types you use repeatedly (web, config, templates)

Use globs when:

* You need to match a specific file name pattern that doesn't correspond to a standard type
* You want to exclude a particular directory: `-g '!vendor/*'`
* You're combining multiple unrelated patterns: `-g '*.txt' -g 'README*'`

Most searches benefit from at least one of these filters. ripgrep's power comes from getting unwanted files out of your search quickly, so you can focus on signal instead of noise.

# Ripgrep File-Type Filtering: A Complete Guide

When you search text for a living, ripgrep's file-type filtering becomes invaluable. Instead of writing the same glob patterns repeatedly—`--glob='*.rs' --glob='*.toml'`—you can simply ask ripgrep to search Rust files with `-trs` or `-trust`. This guide explains how file-type filtering works and how to customize it for your workflows.

## What Are File Types?

Ripgrep ships with predefined file types that map type names to glob patterns. The `rust` type, for example, corresponds to `*.rs`. The `c` type expands to `*.[chH] *.[chH].in *.cats`, covering C source files, headers, and in-files. Each type is a shorthand for one or more glob patterns that identify files of that type.

A file type name must consist only of Unicode letters and numbers—no punctuation. You can see all available types with `--type-list`.

## Filtering By Type With `--type`

The `--type` flag (short form `-t`) restricts your search to files matching a specific type. This is the primary way to narrow your search scope.

### Basic Usage

```bash
rg 'function_name' --type rust
```

This searches only `.rs` files for your pattern. The short form is more convenient:

```bash
rg 'function_name' -trust
```

Multiple types can be combined in a single command. Each type acts as an OR condition—search matches any of the specified types:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type rust --type toml
```

This searches both Rust source files and TOML configuration files.

### Short Form Details

The `-t` flag supports inline specification when followed directly by the type name. `-trust` expands to `--type rust`. You can even chain multiple types: `-trust -ttoml` selects both Rust and TOML files. The form `-t` alone requires the type name as the next argument.

### The Special `all` Type

Ripgrep provides a special type called `all`. When you use `--type all`, ripgrep behaves as if you had passed `--type` for every file type it knows about, including any custom types you've defined. This puts ripgrep into "whitelist mode"—it will only search files it recognizes via type definitions.

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type all
```

This is useful when you want to search only recognized file types and exclude untyped or unrecognized files.

## Excluding Types With `--type-not`

The `--type-not` flag (short form `-T`) is the inverse of `--type`. It excludes files matching a type from your search.

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-not json
```

This searches everything except JSON files. Like `--type`, you can specify multiple exclusions:

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type-not json --type-not xml
```

The short form works the same way as with `--type`:

```bash
rg 'pattern' -Tjson -Txml
```

Or chained:

```bash
rg 'pattern' -Tjson -Txml
```

### Mixing Include and Exclude

You can combine `--type` and `--type-not` in the same command. When mixed, they're applied in order. For example:

```bash
rg 'pattern' -trust --type-not json -ttoml
```

This matches files that are (Rust OR TOML) AND NOT JSON. The flags are processed left-to-right.

### The Special `all` Type for Exclusion

Just as `--type all` enables whitelist mode, `--type-not all` enables blacklist mode—ripgrep will search only files that are *unrecognized* by its type definitions. This is useful when searching untyped scripts or configuration files that don't match any predefined type.

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type-not all
```

## Creating Custom Types With `--type-add`

The `--type-add` flag adds new globs to existing types or defines entirely new types. This is how you extend ripgrep's type system for your own file formats and naming conventions.

### Adding a Single Glob

Define a new type by specifying the type name and a glob pattern, separated by a colon:

```bash
rg 'theme' --type-add 'config:*.conf' --type config
```

This defines a new type `config` matching `*.conf` files, then searches only those files.

### Multiple Globs for One Type

You can add multiple globs to the same type by using `--type-add` multiple times:

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb
```

Or more concisely with brace expansion:

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb
```

Both forms achieve the same result: the `web` type matches any HTML, CSS, or JavaScript file.

### Including Globs From Other Types

The special `include` directive lets you combine existing types into a new one. For example, to create a type that matches source code in multiple languages:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-add 'src:include:rust,python,javascript' -tsrc
```

This defines `src` as matching all files that belong to the `rust`, `python`, and `javascript` types. You can still add additional globs after using include:

```bash
rg 'pattern' --type-add 'src:include:rust,python' --type-add 'src:*.sh' -tsrc
```

Now `src` matches Rust files, Python files, and shell scripts.

### Important: Type-Add Is Per-Invocation

The `--type-add` flag only applies to the current ripgrep command. It does *not* persist to future invocations. If you want a custom type available every time you use ripgrep, you must either:

1. Add it to a shell alias (not recommended for complex setups)
2. Store it in ripgrep's configuration file

## Viewing Available Types With `--type-list`

The `--type-list` flag displays all available types and their corresponding glob patterns. Run it standalone:

```bash
rg --type-list
```

This shows output like:

```
ada: *.adb, *.ads
agda: *.agda, *.lagda
aidl: *.aidl
...
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
...
```

Each line shows a type name followed by a colon and a comma-separated list of globs.

`--type-list` respects any `--type-add` or `--type-clear` flags you provide, so you can see the final set of types and globs that will be used:

```bash
rg --type-add 'mytype:*.custom' --type-list | grep mytype
```

This shows `mytype: *.custom` in the output.

## Clearing Type Definitions With `--type-clear`

The `--type-clear` flag removes all globs previously defined for a type. Once cleared, you can add new globs to that type name. This is useful when you want to redefine an existing type entirely:

```bash
rg --type-clear rust --type-add 'rust:*.rs' --type-add 'rust:*.rsx'
```

This clears the built-in Rust type definition and replaces it with one that also matches `.rsx` files.

Like `--type-add`, `--type-clear` only affects the current invocation and is not persisted.

## Practical Examples

### Example 1: Search Only Tests

If you want to search only test files across your project:

```bash
rg 'assert_eq' --type-add 'test:*_test.rs' --type-add 'test:*_test.py' --type-add 'test:*.test.js' -ttest
```

Or if your types already match your test files, simply:

```bash
rg 'assert' -trusttest -tpytest
```

### Example 2: Search Everything Except Generated Files

When you have generated code mixed with handwritten code:

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-not-all --type-add 'generated:*.pb.rs' --type-add 'generated:*.gen.py' --type-not generated
```

### Example 3: Search "Web Stack" Files

Create a temporary `web` type for HTML, CSS, and JavaScript:

```bash
rg 'function debounce' --type-add 'web:include:javascript,css' --type-add 'web:*.html' -tweb
```

### Example 4: Combine Type Filtering With Glob Patterns

Types and globs both apply to the same search. Globs have lower precedence than type filtering, so you can combine them:

```bash
rg 'pattern' -trust -g '!src/tests/*'
```

This searches Rust files, but excludes anything in `src/tests/` directories.

## Making Types Persistent

Since `--type-add` only applies to the current command, persistence requires configuration. Ripgrep reads a configuration file pointed to by the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable.

Create a configuration file (e.g., `~/.ripgreprc`):

```
# Add a web type
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}

# Add a generated code type
--type-add
generated:*.pb.rs
--type-add
generated:*.gen.py
```

Then set the environment variable:

```bash
export RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH="$HOME/.ripgreprc"
```

Now your custom types are available in every ripgrep invocation. Command-line arguments override configuration file settings, so you can still override or add types on-the-fly.

## How Type Filtering Interacts With Other Ripgrep Features

File-type filtering has lower precedence than both the `--glob` flag and rules from ignore files (`.gitignore`, `.ignore`, `.rgignore`). This means:

- If `.gitignore` excludes a file, it won't be searched even if you specify its type.
- If you provide a `--glob` pattern that contradicts a type filter, glob precedence wins.
- For example, `rg pattern -trust -g '*.rs'` searches only files that are both Rust type *and* match the `*.rs` glob. Since all Rust files match `*.rs`, this is redundant but harmless.

## Conclusion

File-type filtering transforms ripgrep from a tool that requires you to specify patterns repeatedly into one that understands your file structure. By combining predefined types, creating custom types for your workflow, and configuring persistence, you can dramatically reduce the friction of searching the right files. Whether you're searching a polyglot project, working with generated code, or simply want to limit noise in search results, file-type filtering is a core ripgrep skill that pays dividends in speed and accuracy.

# Ripgrep File-Type Filtering: Developer Guide

Ripgrep's file-type filtering system allows users to search only files of specific types (e.g., `rg -t rust pattern`). This guide explains how type definitions are represented, how matchers are constructed, and what contributors need to know about this subsystem.

## Type Definitions

File-type definitions live in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and are represented by the `FileTypeDef` struct:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef {
    name: String,
    globs: Vec<String>,
}
```

A `FileTypeDef` pairs a type name (like `"rust"`) with a vector of glob patterns (like `["*.rs"]`). Multiple globs can belong to a single type. For example, the C type might include patterns `["*.c", "*.h"]` to match both source and header files.

Default type definitions are stored in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs` as a constant array of tuples: `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]`. Each tuple contains an array of name aliases and an array of glob patterns. This design allows a single type to have multiple names—for instance, the C# type has both `"cs"` and `"csharp"` as names, both mapping to the same glob patterns. The `TypesBuilder::add_defaults()` method expands these tuples into individual `FileTypeDef` entries.

## Building a Type Matcher

Type matchers are constructed via `TypesBuilder` in two stages: **definition** and **selection**.

### Stage 1: Definition

The builder accumulates file-type definitions through methods like:

- `add_defaults()` — loads all built-in types
- `add(name, glob)` — adds a single glob pattern to a named type
- `add_def(def)` — parses a string in the form `name:glob` or `name:include:type1,type2`

For example, `add_def("foo:*.foo")` creates a new type `foo` matching `*.foo` files. The include syntax lets you compose types: `add_def("mycombo:include:rust,cpp")` creates `mycombo` that matches any file matching either the `rust` or `cpp` types.

The builder stores these definitions in a `HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` and performs validation—type names must be alphanumeric, and references in include definitions must already exist. This fail-fast approach prevents partial corruption of the type registry.

### Stage 2: Selection

After definitions are registered, users specify which types to match via:

- `select(name)` — include files of this type
- `negate(name)` — exclude files of this type
- Special case: `select("all")` or `negate("all")` applies to all registered types

Selections are stored internally as a `Vec<Selection<()>>`, where `Selection` is an enum:

```rust
enum Selection<T> {
    Select(String, T),
    Negate(String, T),
}
```

The order of selections matters for precedence: the last matching selection wins when building the final matcher.

### Stage 3: Compilation

Calling `build()` converts the definitions and selections into a `Types` matcher:

1. For each selection, the builder looks up its corresponding `FileTypeDef`.
2. Each glob pattern in the definition is compiled into a `Glob` object via `globset::GlobBuilder`, with `literal_separator(true)` enabled to prevent wildcards from matching path separators (e.g., `*.rs` matches `foo.rs` but not `foo/bar.rs`).
3. All compiled globs are combined into a `GlobSet` using `GlobSetBuilder`.
4. A mapping `Vec<(usize, usize)>` is built to track which glob index corresponds to which selection and which glob within that selection's definition.

The resulting `Types` struct contains:

```rust
pub struct Types {
    defs: Vec<FileTypeDef>,              // All definitions, sorted by name
    selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>,  // Globs grouped by selection
    has_selected: bool,                  // True if any Select (not Negate) exists
    glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>,  // Glob index → (selection, glob_within_def)
    set: GlobSet,                        // Compiled glob matcher
    matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>,      // Thread-local storage for match results
}
```

## Matching Files

When a file path is checked against a `Types` matcher via `matched(path, is_dir)`:

1. Directories always return `Match::None` because file-type filtering only applies to files.
2. The file name is extracted from the path (not the full path, only the file name).
3. The `GlobSet` tests the file name against all compiled globs, returning indices of matching globs.
4. The highest-precedence match is the **last one** in the result set, mapping back to its selection via `glob_to_selection`.
5. If the selection is a `Select`, the result is `Match::Whitelist(Glob)`. If it's a `Negate`, the result is `Match::Ignore(Glob)`.
6. If no glob matches but at least one `Select` exists, the file is implicitly ignored (`Match::Ignore`), because selections narrow the search space.
7. Otherwise, the result is `Match::None`, indicating the type matcher has no opinion.

The `Glob` wrapper returned contains the matched `FileTypeDef`, allowing callers to report which type matched.

## Integration into ripgrep

Ripgrep integrates types into its ignore system in `crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`. When checking whether to include a file, the ignore matcher calls `self.types.matched(path, is_dir)` and combines its result with gitignore rules and overrides. Selections of file types effectively act as a whitelist filter when enabled: only files matching the selected types are included.

In the CLI, users provide type selections via flags like `--type rust` (select rust) or `--type-not c` (negate c). The high-level argument builder in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs` parses these and calls the appropriate `TypesBuilder` methods, then calls `build()` to produce the final matcher.

## Key Design Decisions

**Glob matching uses file names only, not full paths.** This simplification makes the system fast and predictable—`*.rs` never matches a directory in the path, only the actual file name. The `literal_separator(true)` option enforces this.

**Selections take precedence by order, with the last match winning.** This matches intuitive expectations: if you specify `-t rust -t c`, the last flag determines precedence if a file matches both (though in practice, a file won't match both unless a composite type includes both).

**When at least one type is selected, non-matching files are ignored.** This differs from negation: `--type rust` means "only show Rust files," while `--type-not c` means "show all files except C files." The `has_selected` flag tracks this distinction.

**Type definitions and selections are separated.** This allows ripgrep to load and validate all types upfront, then resolve selections without re-reading definitions, enabling clear error reporting when a selection references a non-existent type.

## For Contributors

When modifying the type system:

- **Adding new built-in types:** Edit `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. Keep entries sorted lexicographically and lines wrapped to ~79 columns. Test that your globs match expected file names without matching directories in paths.

- **Changing matching logic:** Modify the `matched()` method in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`. Remember that it operates on file names only and that precedence is determined by the last matching glob in the set.

- **Adding features:** Consider whether they belong in `TypesBuilder` (build-time concerns like how types are registered) or `Types` (runtime matching logic). The builder is intentionally stateful to enable fluent API chaining; the matcher is immutable and thread-safe.

- **Testing:** The test module in `types.rs` uses a macro to define match scenarios. It creates type definitions, makes selections, and asserts the final match result. Tests verify both positive matches and non-matches, including the behavior when no selection exists versus when selections are present.

The globset crate (`crates/globset/src/lib.rs`) handles the underlying glob compilation and matching using regex automata for efficiency. It supports standard Unix glob syntax including `*`, `?`, `[...]`, `{a,b}`, and `**`. Changes to glob semantics should be made there, not in the types module.

# Developer Guide: ripgrep's File-Type Filtering

## Overview

ripgrep's file-type filtering system allows users to include or exclude files by type—for example, `rg --type rust pattern` searches only `.rs` files, while `rg --type-add 'foo:*.foo' pattern` adds a custom type. This guide explains how type definitions are stored, how users' selections and negations combine into a matcher, and what you need to know to maintain or extend this subsystem.

## Type Definitions: Representation and Storage

File types in ripgrep are ultimately pairs of a name and a set of glob patterns. The core type is `FileTypeDef` (in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`):

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef {
    name: String,
    globs: Vec<String>,
}
```

For example, the Rust type is defined as `FileTypeDef { name: "rust", globs: vec!["*.rs"] }`, and C files are `FileTypeDef { name: "c", globs: vec!["*.[ch]", "*.[ch].in", "*.cats"] }`.

### Default Types

Default type definitions ship as a compile-time constant array in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["rust"], &["*.rs"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[ch]", "*.[ch].in", "*.cats"]),
    // ... ~250 more types
];
```

Each entry is `(&[name_aliases], &[glob_patterns])`. A single entry can have multiple name aliases (e.g., both `"py"` and `"python"` refer to Python files), and each type can match multiple glob patterns. The constant is kept lexicographically sorted and there's a test enforcing this.

### Runtime Type Storage

When the user or the code calls `TypesBuilder::add_defaults()`, these compile-time entries are unpacked into a `TypesBuilder` struct:

```rust
pub struct TypesBuilder {
    types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<()>>,
}
```

The builder accumulates type definitions in a `HashMap` keyed by name, so later calls to `select()` or `negate()` can reference them by name. Definitions can be overridden by calling `clear()` before re-adding, and new custom definitions are added with `add()`, which takes a name and a glob pattern and pushes it to the globs vector of an existing definition or creates a new one.

### Definition Syntax

The `add_def()` method parses user-provided type definitions in two formats:

1. **Root definitions:** `name:glob` creates a new type matching the given glob. For example, `"foo:*.foo"` defines a type named `foo` matching `*.foo`.

2. **Include definitions:** `name:include:comma,separated,types` creates a new type that includes all patterns from the named types. For example, `"web:include:html,js"` defines a `web` type that matches both HTML and JavaScript files.

Include definitions are resolved at build time: if you include type `X`, the builder clones all of `X`'s patterns into the new type being defined. This means include definitions are not stored as references—they are flattened immediately.

## Building a Matcher: From Selections to GlobSet

### Selections

Before building, users make a series of selections and negations on types. These are stored as `Selection` enums:

```rust
enum Selection<T> {
    Select(String, T),
    Negate(String, T),
}
```

A `Select("rust")` means "match only Rust files"; a `Negate("test")` means "exclude test files". These selections are processed in order during the build—the order matters for precedence, as the "highest precedent" (last) match wins.

### The Build Process

Calling `TypesBuilder::build()` produces a `Types` struct and is where the complex work happens:

```rust
pub struct Types {
    defs: Vec<FileTypeDef>,  // All definitions, sorted
    selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>,  // User selections with resolved defs
    has_selected: bool,  // True if any Select (not Negate) is present
    glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>,  // Maps each glob to its selection
    set: GlobSet,  // The compiled glob set for fast matching
    matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>,  // Thread-local storage for match results
}
```

Here's what `build()` does:

1. **Iterate over selections.** For each `Selection`, look up the corresponding `FileTypeDef` in the builder's HashMap.

2. **For each selection, iterate over its globs.** For every glob pattern in that type's definition, call `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true).build()`. The `literal_separator(true)` flag ensures that `*` and `?` cannot match path separators—this means `*.rs` matches `foo.rs` but not `foo/bar.rs`, which is the expected behavior for filename-based filtering.

3. **Accumulate glob metadata.** Each glob is added to a `GlobSetBuilder`, and a mapping `(selection_index, glob_index_within_type)` is stored in `glob_to_selection`. This allows the matcher to later trace a matched glob back to the selection that contributed it.

4. **Build the GlobSet.** Call `build_set.build()` to compile all globs into a single `GlobSet`. This is owned by `regex_automata` and uses DFA/NFA techniques to match multiple patterns in a single pass.

5. **Record whether there are any positive selections.** If `has_selected` is true (i.e., at least one `Select` is present), then files matching no selected type are treated as ignored. If `has_selected` is false (only `Negate` was used), then unmatched files are treated as neither ignored nor whitelisted (`Match::None`).

### Key Design Choice: Literal Separators

The `literal_separator(true)` setting is critical: it prevents glob wildcards from matching across directory boundaries. Without it, `*.rs` could match a file at any depth in the tree. This design ensures that type filtering applies only to filename matching, not path structure.

## The Matching Algorithm

The `Types::matched()` method, called at search time with a file path, performs matching:

```rust
pub fn matched<'a, P: AsRef<Path>>(
    &'a self,
    path: P,
    is_dir: bool,
) -> Match<Glob<'a>>
```

1. **Directories are never matched.** If `is_dir` is true, return `Match::None` immediately. Type filtering applies only to files.

2. **Extract the filename.** Call `file_name(path)` to get only the basename (e.g., `"foo.rs"` from `"/path/to/foo.rs"`). If there's no filename and `has_selected` is true, return `Match::Ignore` (since selections don't match, it's implicitly ignored). If `has_selected` is false and there's no filename, return `Match::None`.

3. **Match against the GlobSet.** Call `self.set.matches_into(name, &mut *matches)`, where `matches` is a reusable thread-local `Vec<usize>` obtained from a `Pool`. This populates the vector with the indices of all matching globs in ascending order.

4. **Determine precedence.** The highest precedent match is the last one in the vector. Look it up: extract the selection index from `glob_to_selection[i]`, retrieve `self.selections[isel]`, and check if it's a `Select` or `Negate`:
   - If `Select`, return `Match::Whitelist`.
   - If `Negate`, return `Match::Ignore`.

5. **Handle no match.** If the vector is empty, return `Match::Ignore` if `has_selected`, otherwise `Match::None`.

This algorithm ensures that negations override selections if they come later, and that the last glob to match determines the result.

## The Match Enum

The result of matching is a `Match<Glob<'a>>` enum (defined in `crates/ignore/src/lib.rs`):

```rust
pub enum Match<T> {
    None,       // No glob matched
    Ignore(T),  // Matched a negation or no selections apply
    Whitelist(T),  // Matched a selection
}
```

The type parameter `T` carries metadata—in the types module, it's `Glob<'a>`, which holds a reference to the matching `FileTypeDef`. This allows the caller to learn which type definition was responsible for the match.

## What Contributors Need to Know

### Adding New Default Types

New entries in `DEFAULT_TYPES` must:

- Use a name that contains only alphanumeric characters (validated by `add()`).
- Include at least one glob pattern.
- Be inserted in lexicographically sorted order (a test enforces this).
- Use the smallest sensible glob set (e.g., don't add `*.bak` to every type; keep types specific).

To add or update a type, edit `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`, run the test suite (particularly the lexicographic sort test), and verify against real-world examples.

### Modifying Type Matching Semantics

The glob compilation step is where subtle bugs live:

- **`literal_separator(true)` is mandatory** for filename-based matching. Removing it would allow wildcards to cross directory boundaries, breaking the expected semantics.
- **Glob patterns are matched against the filename only**, extracted by `file_name()`. If you need to match paths (e.g., to include specific directories), that belongs in the ignore system, not the types system.
- **Glob precedence** is last-wins within a selection set. If you're adding support for more complex precedence (e.g., between types), ensure the `glob_to_selection` mapping is still correct.

### Thread Safety

`Types` is `Clone` and thread-safe. The reusable `Vec<usize>` pool (`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`) is a performance optimization to avoid allocating a new vector on every match. The pool is thread-safe by design—each thread holds its own `Vec` until it's returned.

### Testing

Tests live in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and use a macro to construct combinations of type definitions and selections, then verify the results. When adding tests:

- Use `matched!()` for positive matches (expecting the file to be included).
- Use `matched!(not, ...)` for negative matches (expecting the file to be excluded).
- Create simple definitions inline rather than relying on defaults for clarity.
- Test both `Select` and `Negate` modes.
- Test include definitions (`name:include:...`) and overlapping types.

### Error Handling

Errors during type building are captured in `Error` variants:

- `UnrecognizedFileType(String)` is raised if a selection refers to a type that doesn't exist.
- `InvalidDefinition` is raised if a definition string doesn't parse or if an include references a nonexistent type.
- `Glob { glob, err }` is raised if a glob pattern fails to compile (e.g., unclosed character class).

The builder returns `Result<Types, Error>`, and errors should propagate to the user rather than panic.

## Performance Considerations

- **GlobSet is fast.** It uses DFA/NFA techniques and short-circuits: if a literal match is found, no regex is executed.
- **Filename extraction is lazy.** Only done if matching might occur (empty set is checked first).
- **Pool reuse matters.** On high-throughput searches (millions of files), the thread-local `Vec` pool avoids malloc churn.
- **Selections are linear.** The builder iterates over selections once during build, then matching is O(number of matched globs), which is typically small.

## Integration with ripgrep's CLI

The types system is used by ripgrep's CLI to handle flags like `--type`, `--type-add`, and `--type-not`. The CLI parses these into selections and negations, calls `TypesBuilder::add_defaults()` and `add_def()` as needed, then calls `build()` to create the matcher. This matcher is then passed to the recursive directory walker, which calls `matched()` for each file.

For implementation details on how the CLI wires this up, see `crates/cli` or `src/args.rs` in ripgrep's main binary.

# Ripgrep File-Type Filtering: Developer Documentation

## Overview

Ripgrep's file-type filtering system allows users to search only files matching specific patterns, such as Rust source files (`.rs`) or Python scripts (`.py`). This system is implemented in the `ignore` crate and provides a flexible, reusable mechanism for matching file paths against named type definitions. The system supports both built-in types and user-defined custom types.

## Type Definitions

### Representation

File type definitions are represented as `FileTypeDef` structs (found in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`):

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef {
    name: String,
    globs: Vec<String>,
}
```

A `FileTypeDef` has two components:

- **name**: A unique identifier for the type (e.g., `"rust"`, `"python"`). Names must be alphanumeric; the special name `"all"` is reserved and refers to all defined types at once.
- **globs**: A vector of glob patterns that match file names belonging to this type. For example, the Rust type includes `["*.rs"]`, while the C type includes `["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]`.

### Default Types

Ripgrep ships with a comprehensive set of default type definitions stored in `DEFAULT_TYPES` (in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`). This constant is a slice of tuples, where each tuple contains an array of type names and an array of glob patterns:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["rust"], &["*.rs"]),
    (&["c"], &["*.[chH]", "*.[chH].in", "*.cats"]),
    (&["cpp"], &["*.[ChH]", "*.cc", "*.[ch]pp", ...]),
    // ...
];
```

Multiple names can refer to the same set of globs (e.g., `"batch"` and `"bat"` both match `"*.bat"`), and globs are often combined using character classes and braces (e.g., `*.[chH]` matches `.c`, `.h`, and `.H` files).

### Custom Type Definitions

Users can add custom type definitions in two ways:

1. **Direct glob patterns**: Using `TypesBuilder::add(name, pattern)`, where the pattern is a single glob.
2. **Include-style definitions**: Using `TypesBuilder::add_def("name:include:type1,type2")` to compose a new type from existing types.

The second form is parsed by looking for the `include:` keyword and expanding it to include all globs from the referenced types. For example, `"web:include:html,css,javascript"` creates a new type that matches files from all three referenced types.

## Building a Matcher

### The TypesBuilder Pattern

Creating a type matcher involves four steps:

1. **Instantiate a builder**: `TypesBuilder::new()` creates an empty builder.
2. **Add type definitions**: Use `add_defaults()` to load built-in types, or `add()` / `add_def()` to add custom ones.
3. **Configure selections**: Use `select(name)` to match files of a type, or `negate(name)` to exclude files of a type.
4. **Build**: Call `build()` to construct the final `Types` matcher.

```rust
let mut builder = TypesBuilder::new();
builder.add_defaults();
builder.select("rust");      // Include Rust files
builder.negate("test");      // Exclude test files
let matcher = builder.build()?;
```

### Internal Representation

The `build()` method constructs a `Types` struct (in `types.rs`), which contains:

- **defs**: A sorted vector of all defined type definitions.
- **selections**: A vector of `Selection<FileTypeDef>` enums, representing the user's choices.
- **has_selected**: A boolean flag indicating whether at least one type is actively selected (as opposed to only negations).
- **glob_to_selection**: A mapping from glob indices in the compiled set to (selection index, glob index) pairs.
- **set**: A `GlobSet` compiled from all selected globs.
- **matches**: A thread-local pool of vectors for reusing allocations during matching.

The `Selection<T>` enum distinguishes between selections (whitelist) and negations (blacklist):

```rust
enum Selection<T> {
    Select(String, T),
    Negate(String, T),
}
```

### GlobSet Construction

During `build()`, all globs from all selections are added to a `GlobSetBuilder` (from the `globset` crate). Each glob is wrapped with `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)`, which treats `/` as a literal character rather than a wildcard separator. The compiled `GlobSet` is used for fast multi-pattern matching.

## Matching Process

### File Name Extraction

Matching operates on the file name component of a path, not the full path. The `file_name()` function (in `crates/ignore/src/pathutil.rs`) extracts this:

- On Unix, it finds the last `/` and returns everything after it as an `OsStr`.
- On Windows, it delegates to `Path::file_name()`.
- It returns `None` for paths ending in `.`, `..`, or containing no file component.

This design ensures consistent matching regardless of directory depth and avoids treating separators in directory names as glob wildcards.

### Match Semantics

When `Types::matched(path, is_dir)` is called:

1. **Skip directories**: Directories return `Match::None` (no filtering applied).
2. **Extract file name**: The path's file name component is extracted; if it doesn't exist and selections are active, the path is ignored.
3. **Glob matching**: The file name is tested against the compiled `GlobSet`, which returns all matching glob indices.
4. **Precedence resolution**: The highest-precedent match (the last in the list) determines the result:
   - If the match is from a `Select`, return `Match::Whitelist(glob_info)`.
   - If the match is from a `Negate`, return `Match::Ignore(glob_info)`.
5. **Fallback behavior**: If no globs matched:
   - If selections are active (i.e., `has_selected` is true), return `Match::Ignore` (reject by default).
   - Otherwise, return `Match::None` (no filter applied).

The `Match<T>` enum (defined in `crates/ignore/src/lib.rs`) has three variants:

```rust
pub enum Match<T> {
    None,
    Ignore(T),
    Whitelist(T),
}
```

Helper methods like `is_ignore()`, `is_whitelist()`, and `is_none()` simplify checking results.

## Key Design Points for Contributors

### Precedence and Order

Glob precedence is determined by insertion order in the `selections` vector. The highest-precedent glob is always the last match found in the `GlobSet`. This allows later selections to override earlier ones, a design pattern inherited from tools like `.gitignore`.

For example, if a user does `builder.select("rust"); builder.negate("test");`, a file like `test.rs` would match both selections, but the negation takes effect because it was added last.

### Thread Safety

The `matches` field uses `Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` to provide thread-local storage of temporary vectors. This allows the matcher to be shared across threads (it implements `Clone` and `Send`) without allocating new vectors per match. Contributors should be aware that matching mutates this pool but does not race (the pool uses thread-local storage).

### Performance Considerations

- **GlobSet compilation**: The cost of building a `Types` is amortized across many matches, so building is intentionally separate from matching.
- **File name extraction**: Matching only operates on the file name, not the full path, reducing the amount of data scanned by globs.
- **Glob pooling**: Reusing temporary vectors in the pool reduces allocation overhead for patterns with many matches.

### Adding or Modifying Type Definitions

To add new default types:

1. Edit `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs` and add your type to the `DEFAULT_TYPES` array.
2. Follow the existing format: `(&["type_name"], &["*.ext1", "*.ext2", ...])`.
3. Keep the list sorted lexicographically.
4. Test by building a matcher with your new type: `builder.add_defaults(); builder.select("your_type");`.

Ensure that glob patterns are unambiguous and don't conflict with other types unexpectedly.

### Error Handling

The system provides two main error cases:

- **UnrecognizedFileType**: Returned when a selection or negation references a type name that doesn't exist in the builder.
- **Glob error**: Returned when a glob pattern is invalid (e.g., unclosed braces).

Contributors should handle these in the calling code, as they indicate configuration problems that users must fix.

## Practical Example

```rust
use ignore::types::TypesBuilder;

// Create a builder and load defaults
let mut builder = TypesBuilder::new();
builder.add_defaults();

// Add a custom type for documentation files
builder.add("docs", "*.md")?;
builder.add("docs", "*.txt")?;

// Select Rust and documentation files
builder.select("rust");
builder.select("docs");

// Build the matcher
let matcher = builder.build()?;

// Use it
assert!(matcher.matched("src/main.rs", false).is_whitelist());
assert!(matcher.matched("README.md", false).is_whitelist());
assert!(matcher.matched("src/main.c", false).is_ignore());
```

## Testing and Debugging

The `types.rs` module includes comprehensive tests (at the end of the file) that verify:

- Selection and negation logic
- Composite type definitions (include-style)
- Edge cases like conflicting selections and negations
- Invalid definitions

When debugging type matching, consider:

1. **Verify type definitions exist**: Use `matcher.definitions()` to list all loaded types.
2. **Check the Match result**: Use `match.is_ignore()`, `match.is_whitelist()`, or `match.is_none()`.
3. **Inspect the glob that matched**: Call `match.inner()?.file_type_def()?.globs()` to see which pattern matched.

Contributors modifying the types system should add tests for new behavior and ensure existing tests continue to pass.
